findings.title: Pin and verify installer script instead of curl | sh in build
findings.whyItBreaks: The new layer executes arbitrary, unpinned shell downloaded from a third-party host at image build time, as root, on the Alpine base. `-L` means curl will follow a cross-origin redirect and execute whatever that second host returns, and there is no checksum/signature, so a compromise or DNS/TLS-level substitution of example.com (or a change to the script upstream) is baked into every image built from this commit and shipped to production — with no rebuild pin to roll back to. It also makes the build non-hermetic: the same commit produces different images depending on what the endpoint returns that day (and, because the layer is cached, different images depending on when it was last built).

findings.title: curl failure is silently swallowed; image builds without the install
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -s` suppresses error output and is used without `-f/--fail`, and the RUN shell's exit status comes from the last pipeline element (`sh`), not curl. So (a) a connection/DNS/TLS failure yields curl's non-zero exit discarded by the pipeline, `sh` reads empty stdin and exits 0; and (b) a 404/5xx response body (an HTML error page) is piped straight into `sh`. In both cases the build reports success at line 3 and proceeds to `COPY app /app` / `CMD ["/app"]`, producing an image in which the component this step was supposed to install is missing or half-installed. A failed install becomes indistinguishable from a successful one and is only discovered at container runtime.

findings.title: Do not execute an unverified remote script in the Dockerfile build
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes arbitrary remote code as root inside the image build with no version pin, no checksum/signature verification, and no TLS-pinning. Whoever controls the response to that URL (endpoint owner, any CDN/DNS/TLS interception path, or the domain if it is a placeholder that someone else registers) controls every image produced from this commit, and the injected code is baked into all downstream layers (`COPY app /app`) and every running container. The URL is `example.com`, an IANA-reserved documentation domain, which cannot legitimately serve install.sh — so this reads as an unfinished placeholder shipping straight into the build path.

findings.title: curl download failure is silently lost; RUN succeeds installing nothing
findings.whyItBreaks: Docker's default shell is `/bin/sh -c` (BusyBox ash on alpine:3.18) with no pipefail, so the pipeline's exit status is that of the last command, `sh` — not `curl`. `curl` is also invoked without `-f`, so an HTTP 4xx/5xx is not even an error for curl. Two concrete wrong outcomes: (a) DNS/connect/TLS failure or an empty response → curl writes nothing, `sh` reads empty stdin and exits 0 → the RUN layer succeeds, Docker caches it as "installed", and the image ships missing whatever install.sh was supposed to install, failing later at container runtime with no build-time signal; (b) the endpoint returns an HTML error page → that HTML is fed to `sh`, producing an opaque syntax-error failure unrelated to the real cause. A failed supply step and a completed supply step are indistinguishable to every consumer of this layer.

findings.title: Do not pipe a remote install script into sh during image build
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes whatever bytes that URL returns, with no checksum, no signature, no version/tag pin, and no digest. The server (or any intermediary/DNS/CDN compromise, or the domain itself — `example.com` is an IANA-reserved documentation domain, so this is either a shipped placeholder or someone else's host) controls arbitrary code that runs as root inside the build (no `USER` in this Dockerfile) and is then baked permanently into every published image, including its filesystem state and any secrets present as build args/mounts. Because Docker caches the RUN layer, the resulting image is also non-reproducible: two builds at different times can produce different binaries with the same Dockerfile, and there is no way to audit what was installed. `-s` suppresses progress/errors and `-L` silently follows redirects to any other host, widening the trust surface.

findings.title: curl failure is swallowed by the pipe, so a broken install builds "successfully"
findings.whyItBreaks: Docker executes RUN via `/bin/sh -c`, which does not set `pipefail`. The exit status of the whole line is therefore `sh`'s, not curl's: DNS failure, TLS failure, connection reset, or an HTTP 404/5xx page all leave curl writing nothing (and without `-f/--fail`, even a 404 response body is emitted with exit 0 while a truncated connection may still exit non-zero) while `sh` reads empty or garbage stdin and can exit 0. The build then succeeds and an image is published with the install step silently missing or partially applied — failure and "installed correctly" are indistinguishable to CI, to the image tag, and to every downstream consumer of the persisted artifact. Nothing in the Dockerfile records what the script was supposed to produce, so there is no later assertion that would catch the omission.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing, conflating missing key with empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: Load's only failure mode is ErrMissing (src/store.go:9-11) and it also returns "" as the value on that path. LoadOrDefault drops the error (_ at line 16) and returns that "" verbatim, so for m = {} (key absent) and for m = {"k": ""} (key present, empty value — a legal entry in map[string]string) the function returns the identical result. Every eventual caller is FORCED to conflate 'no value configured' with 'value explicitly set to empty', so any config-default / fallback / persistence decision built on this public API silently takes the wrong branch; the failure signal cannot be recovered by any means, including logging, because it is discarded inside the helper. The same hunk is also a contract mismatch: the exported name promises "OrDefault", but the signature accepts no default parameter, so the only 'default' a caller can ever get is the empty string.

findings.title: Propagate or default on Load's error instead of discarding it
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) for an absent key and ("", nil) for a key present with an empty value (src/store.go:7-13). LoadOrDefault drops the error (line 16: v, _ := Load(...)) and returns "" in both cases, so every eventual caller receives a value that is observably identical whether or not the key exists. Any caller that persists, caches, or acts on the result will silently treat "key not configured" as "configured as empty" — a lost error signal shipped as a real value. The contract defect is present now, independent of callers (rg shows zero call sites today). Separately, the carrier name promises a default, but the signature takes no default argument, so the "default" is hard-coded to the zero value "" and callers cannot specify a non-empty fallback — the name over-states what lines 16-17 compute.

findings.title: Do not swallow ErrMissing in exported LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Load signals a failed lookup only through ErrMissing and returns "" on that path (src/store.go:10). LoadOrDefault drops the error (`v, _ := Load(...)` @ src/store.go:16) and returns the same "" that a successfully-loaded key holding an empty value returns (src/store.go:12). Because the helper is exported and returns only a string, ErrMissing becomes unobservable through this path: every eventual caller is forced to conflate "lookup failed / key absent" with "value is legitimately empty", so a missing config/record silently degrades to the empty string instead of erroring — and a name promising a *default* hands back the Go zero value with no way for the caller to supply or detect anything else. There is no log at the swallow site, so the failure is lost, not merely deferred.

findings.title: Run returns before sends complete; caller's close(results) can panic
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change Run was synchronous: every 'results <- j*2' completed in the caller's goroutine, so Run returning was the guarantee that all results had been delivered. That is the contract an exported func with a 'chan<- int' sink parameter implies, and it is what lets the (idiomatic) owner of the channel write 'Run(...); close(results)'. Now Run returns as soon as the goroutines are spawned, while the sends are still in flight. Any caller following the old contract races close(results) against a pending send -> runtime panic 'send on closed channel' in a goroutine the caller cannot recover from or even identify. The change also gives the caller no way to detect completion: there is no WaitGroup, no returned done channel, and nothing is closed when the last result is sent, so a reader looping 'for range results' either terminates early (first consumer that sees the channel drained closes it) or blocks forever. There are no in-repo callers to absorb this, but Run is exported from package worker, so the contract break ships now.

findings.title: ctx is never consulted; abandoned consumer leaks len(jobs) goroutines
findings.whyItBreaks: The spawn loop ignores ctx entirely and does a bare blocking send. If the consumer stops reading (context cancelled, handler timeout, early return from a 'select' on ctx.Done()), each in-flight goroutine parks forever on 'results <- j*2' — and unlike the old code, the goroutine is no longer the caller's own, so nothing the caller does afterwards can wake it; it holds the channel alive and leaks one goroutine per undrained job (up to len(jobs), unbounded since one goroutine is spawned per job with no pool or semaphore). Worse, if the caller cancels and then closes results, those parked senders become the panicked senders of finding 1. The function still advertises cancellation by accepting a context.Context that it never reads.

findings.title: Run returns before spawned goroutines send; add WaitGroup
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change every send happened on the caller's goroutine, so Run returning implied len(jobs) values were already produced and the function had a well-defined completion point. Now Run returns as soon as it has spawned the goroutines, with zero synchronization, so the caller cannot tell when the work is done: (a) the idiomatic `worker.Run(ctx, jobs, ch); close(ch)` — and any wrapper that closes a channel, releases a pooled buffer, or publishes the collected results once Run returns — races the in-flight goroutines and produces an unrecoverable 'send on closed channel' panic in a goroutine nobody can recover; (b) if the process/main returns while goroutines are still blocked on an unbuffered send, remaining results are dropped silently with no error signal; (c) the goroutines are orphaned — the caller holds no handle (Run returns nothing) and ctx, which is already ignored at line 5, cannot stop them, so they block forever on a channel whose reader is gone. Additionally, per-job fan-out is unbounded, so a large `jobs` slice spawns one goroutine per element instead of the previous bounded, sequential producer.

findings.title: Make Run wait for spawned result senders before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base version each `results <- j*2` executed on Run's own goroutine, so Run returning guaranteed all len(jobs) values were already handed off (with a buffered channel) or accepted by a live receiver. After this change, Run returns as soon as the N goroutines are spawned; the sends are still pending and are not tracked anywhere (no WaitGroup, no done channel, and the pre-existing `ctx` is still unused, so there is no cancellation path either). Every canonical consumer of this exported API breaks: (a) `Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` — the pattern needed to terminate a `for r := range results` reader — now races with the detached senders and can panic with "send on closed channel" or leave values unwritten; (b) a caller that shuts down / closes the channel / returns early after Run() observes a completion that has not happened; (c) if a reader stops consuming, all remaining senders block forever on `results <-` and can never be cancelled or joined, so the work is silently leaked while Run reports success. This is a run-to-completion/tracking regression introduced by the changed lines, not a pre-existing issue.

findings.title: OR in canDeleteRecord lets non-admins delete tenant records
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing `&&` with `||` makes either operand alone sufficient to grant deletion. Two distinct regressions on this one line: (1) `session.isAdmin=false` with `session.tenantId===record.tenantId` now returns true, so every ordinary member of a tenant can delete records belonging to other users in that tenant — `RecordRef.ownerId` (src/permissions.ts:9) is never consulted, so tenant membership becomes a blanket delete right; base (6f9a947:src/permissions.ts:13) rejected this. (2) `session.isAdmin=true` with a different `tenantId` now returns true, so an administrator scoped to tenant A can delete tenant B's records — a cross-tenant privilege escape that base explicitly blocked. Both paths persist a destructive write (record deletion) on an incorrect authorization decision; this is an exported public predicate with no in-repo caller that could re-narrow it, so every consumer inherits the bypass.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord || bypasses tenant isolation and admin requirement
findings.whyItBreaks: Base semantics were `isAdmin AND sameTenant`, i.e. admin is a precondition and tenant equality is an independent, always-required isolation check. With `||`, either operand alone grants deletion, producing two new authorized paths that did not exist before: (1) `session.isAdmin === true` short-circuits the tenant comparison, so an admin of tenant A passes for a `RecordRef` in tenant B — multi-tenant isolation bypass / cross-tenant data destruction; (2) `session.tenantId === record.tenantId` passes with `isAdmin === false`, so every ordinary user can delete every record in their tenant, including records whose `ownerId` belongs to another user (ownerId is never consulted anywhere in the function). Both are silent, unpersisted-to-decision escalations on a destructive operation, and the function is exported, so every consumer of the library inherits the widened grant without any call-site change.

findings.title: Restore tenant+admin conjunction in canDeleteRecord authorization gate
findings.whyItBreaks: Base gate was `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId` — deletion required tenant containment AND an admin role. With `||`, two previously-deny combinations now return true: (a) isAdmin=false, same tenantId → true, so every ordinary tenant member passes the gate for ANY record in the tenant, including records whose RecordRef.ownerId belongs to someone else (ownerId is part of the contract at lines 7-10 but is never read); (b) isAdmin=true, different tenantId → true, so a tenant-local admin can delete other tenants' records — cross-tenant destruction. Because this is the exported authorization predicate, every caller trusts `true` as 'this session may delete this record'; there is no residual check inside the function, so both paths produce unauthorized deletions (irreversible data loss) rather than a degrade-with-error path.

findings.title: Fix corrupt settings then save: defaults overwrite user's real settings
findings.whyItBreaks: updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:19-23) is a read-modify-write path: it calls parseSettings(raw), mutates fontSize, and unconditionally calls save(JSON.stringify(settings)). At base, any parse/validation failure threw out of parseSettings before save() ran, so a corrupt, partially-written, newer-schema, or non-object settings file was left untouched and the caller saw an error. With the new catch-all, the failure is replaced by {...DEFAULTS}, so the same call now writes {"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>} over the original file. Concrete regression: a user whose settings file is temporarily unreadable/invalid (editor crash, truncated write, settings written by a newer build) changes the font size once and loses their theme and every other stored setting, with no error surfaced anywhere. Failure-as-value is also indistinguishable from a legitimate {theme:"light",fontSize:14} because the function still returns type Settings with no null/throw signal.

findings.title: Public parseSettings contract drops its error signal to a valid-looking value
findings.whyItBreaks: parseSettings is an exported API whose declared return type is unchanged (Settings, non-nullable), but its behaviour changed from 'throws on invalid input' to 'returns DEFAULTS on any input'. The catch is unqualified, so it also swallows programming errors that base let propagate (SyntaxError from JSON.parse, TypeError when raw parses to null/a number/a string, e.g. parseSettings('null')). Callers therefore cannot distinguish 'user explicitly wants light/14' from 'settings file is unreadable/invalid', which is exactly the signal a settings UI needs to show 'your config is invalid' or to keep defaults out of a write-back. The contract is unusable as shipped, independent of whether other call-sites exist in this repo yet.

findings.title: Stop swallowing parse/validation errors in exported parseSettings
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version's contract was 'parseSettings throws on unparseable or invalid settings' (throw sites at old lines 9-11). The new try/catch maps every failure — JSON syntax error, missing/typed-wrong theme, missing/typed-wrong fontSize — to { ...DEFAULTS } with no log and no error channel. Because parseSettings is exported (line 8), every caller is forced to conflate 'settings were read successfully' with 'settings were unreadable/invalid': the return value is identical in both cases. Concretely, parseSettings('{"theme":"dark"}') now returns { theme: "light", fontSize: 14 } — the user's explicit theme choice is silently reverted and nothing anywhere records that the load failed, so a corrupt settings file becomes an invisible, non-reproducible 'my settings reset themselves' state instead of an actionable error.

findings.title: updateFontSize must not save when settings failed to parse
findings.whyItBreaks: updateFontSize has no way to detect a failed load once parseSettings stops throwing, so the swallow at line 15 turns a read failure into a write. Base behavior: save was never called with unparsable/invalid raw (the throw propagated out of line 20). Head behavior: for raw = '{"theme":"dark","fontSize":20,"experimental":true}' (or any malformed/typed-wrong payload, e.g. fontSize: "20"), parseSettings returns {theme:'light',fontSize:14}, line 21 sets fontSize to size, and line 22 persists that — permanently overwriting the user's real settings file with defaults plus one field, losing theme and every unmodeled key. That is user-initiated, non-undoable data loss with no error shown to the user.

findings.title: Stop parseSettings swallowing errors; defaults get saved over real settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The new `catch { return { ...DEFAULTS }; }` (lines 14-16) discards every failure signal that base propagated: JSON.parse throwing on malformed raw, and the function's own `bad theme` / `bad fontSize` validation throws (lines 11-12 are now caught by the same try, so the validation is unreachable as a signal). Callers can no longer distinguish "config is corrupt/invalid" from "config legitimately says light/14". The concrete wrong behavior happens in this same file: `updateFontSize` (line 20) takes the returned defaults, sets fontSize, and at line 22 calls `save(JSON.stringify(settings))` — so a user whose stored config is unreadable/invalid (e.g. `{"theme":"dark","fontSize":"16"}`, a truncated write, a stray BOM) has their theme silently rewritten to `"light"` and any extra keys dropped, instead of the previous behavior where the throw aborted before any write. That is a silent overwrite of persisted user state. parseSettings is exported, so every external importer inherits the same unusable contract.

findings.title: Revert pageCount to Math.ceil; floor drops the final partial page
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported name/contract of pageCount(totalItems, pageSize) is "how many pages are needed to hold totalItems", but Math.floor(totalItems / pageSize) computes only the number of *whole* pages. Substituting real values: pageCount(10,3) previously returned 4, now returns 3 — items 10 (the 3.34th page) are unreachable; pageCount(1,50) now returns 0 for a non-empty collection; pageCount(99,10) returns 9 instead of 10. Any caller that loops page 1..pageCount (the only sane use of this API) terminates one page early and silently loses the last up-to-(pageSize-1) records: no throw, no error signal, just a short/incomplete listing. Exact multiples (e.g. 9,3) are unaffected, which is exactly why this regression survives naive smoke tests. The change is also lossless-reversible in intent: nothing in the repo (no caller, doc, type, or test) requests a whole-page count, so there is no legitimate behavior this fix implements.

findings.title: buildReport mixes two builds: artifacts from hardcoded "verified" ref
findings.whyItBreaks: Before the change, artifacts were resolved from the same commit reported as builtFrom (build.ref(branch) -> artifactsAt(commit)). Now line 13 resolves a second, caller-uncontrollable ref name ("verified") and line 14 feeds it to artifactsAt while builtFrom still carries the branch commit. The exported BuildReport contract promises one build's data; consumers get builtFrom=<branch commit> paired with artifacts belonging to a different commit, and the branch parameter silently stops governing the artifact list — so buildReport("feature-x") returns feature-x's commit stamped on verified's artifact set. No error is raised, so a wrong/polluted build record is persisted and published silently, and any caller that verifies artifacts against builtFrom will either fail closed (blocking every non-verified branch) or, worse, accept mismatched artifacts.

findings.title: Report artifacts resolved from a different commit than builtFrom
findings.whyItBreaks: Before the change, builtFrom and artifacts were guaranteed to describe the same commit (both derived from build.ref(branch)). Now `verified` is resolved from the literal ref name "verified" — a magic string that exists nowhere else in the repo or in its git history — while `commit` is still resolved from the caller-supplied `branch` and is still what `builtFrom` reports. The exported BuildReport interface (src/report.ts:5-8) promises a single build; any consumer that reads report.artifacts as "the artifacts of report.builtFrom" (release listing, provenance/attestation, download UI) now silently receives the artifact set of an unrelated commit, i.e. artifacts mis-attributed to a commit that never produced them. Additionally, `ref(name): string` has no error channel: if "verified" does not resolve in a given repository, the unresolved value is passed straight into artifactsAt, and an empty result is indistinguishable from "this build produced no artifacts" — the report would then be emitted/persisted as a legitimate artifact-free build instead of a failed lookup.

findings.title: Keep artifacts and builtFrom on the same resolved commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The only change to the exported buildReport body is the argument of artifactsAt: previously build.artifactsAt(commit) (line 13 of base, same commit as builtFrom), now build.artifactsAt(build.ref("verified")). BuildReport.builtFrom (src/report.ts:7) still carries the branch-resolved commit, so every consumer that pairs the two fields — "the artifacts of this build" — now receives artifact names from an unrelated, non-parameterized ref while the label says branch@commit. On any branch whose ref != "verified" (feature branch, release cut, hotfix), the report lists artifacts that were not built from builtFrom, which is exactly the association a build report exists to assert. Callers also lose all control over the ref: `branch` now only affects the label, and a missing/renamed "verified" ref (Build.ref returns a plain string, src/report.ts:2, with no error channel) yields empty-or-wrong artifacts with nothing to detect it against builtFrom.

findings.title: Restore the slice cap in recentEntries
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff drops `.slice(0, limit)`, so for every limit > 0 the function returns ALL reversed entries. Line 1 still promises 'Returns at most `limit` entries' and the parameter is still named `limit`, so callers trust the cap. The in-repo caller renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9-12) does `const page = recentEntries(all, 20)` and allocates `new Array<string>(20)`, then writes `out[i]` for every `i < page.length`; with more than 20 entries the page is uncapped, `out` silently grows to `all.length`, and the feed returns the whole history instead of one page (unbounded output size/memory for any caller that renders the result). For any external importer of this exported helper, the contract is now broken regardless of call-site count.

findings.title: Restore slice(0, limit) in recentEntries; limit is currently inert
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaced `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)` with `const sorted = [...all].reverse(); ... return sorted;` (src/feed.ts:3-5). The `limit <= 0` guard covers only non-positive values; for every positive `limit` the full reversed array is returned, contradicting the unchanged public contract at src/feed.ts:1 ('Returns at most `limit` entries, newest first'). Verified relying caller: renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9) calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` and pre-allocates `new Array<string>(20)` (src/feed.ts:10), then writes `out[i]` for `i < page.length` (src/feed.ts:11) — with all.length > 20, page.length is now all.length, so out grows past 20 and renderFeed returns the whole feed rather than a 20-item page. On upgrade this is an unbounded-output regression (oversized page/payload, memory growth proportional to the entire history) with no cap the caller can enforce.

findings.title: Restore the missing slice cap in recentEntries
findings.whyItBreaks: The new body only adds an early `limit <= 0` return and then returns `sorted`, i.e. the entire reversed input, so the `limit` argument has no effect for every limit >= 1. Line 1's doc contract ("Returns at most `limit` entries, newest first") is unchanged and is the public contract of this exported function, and there is a live relying caller: `renderFeed` @ src/feed.ts:9-11 treats `recentEntries(all, 20)` as a page of at most 20 and writes it into a length-20 buffer. With more than 20 entries the returned feed is now the full, unbounded history (all N items, buffer silently grown past its declared size), i.e. pagination/clamping disappears for every consumer of this API rather than being capped.

findings.title: Make entry-count header match the emitted (non-stale) rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 20 drops stale entries from the body, but line 22 still passes `entries.length` to `headerLines`, which writes it as `# entry-count:` (src/manifest.ts:15). Before this change every entry was rendered, so the header count was always equal to the row count; now it is larger by the number of stale entries. Any consumer of this exported public renderer that trusts the declared count — a parser that reads exactly N rows, a reader that asserts `entry-count` equals the number of manifest lines for integrity verification, or one that waits for N entries — under-reads, blocks, or rejects a valid manifest as truncated/corrupt as soon as a single stale entry exists. With all entries stale the emitted file is header-only with `# entry-count: N` and zero rows, i.e. the artifact's own metadata denies its contents. Failure mode is silent: renderManifest cannot signal it, the disagreement is only visible to the reader.

findings.title: Make `# entry-count` header count emitted (non-stale) rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The body of the artifact changed (stale entries are dropped at line 20-21) but the header metadata still advertises the unfiltered total: line 22 calls `headerLines(opts, entries.length)`, and `headerLines` writes `# entry-count: ${count}` (line 15). For any manifest containing at least one stale entry the declared count is larger than the number of records actually present. Consumers of a header-then-N-records format either block on EOF while waiting for the missing rows or, if reading from a stream/multi-document source, consume the following unrelated line as a record — i.e. mis-parsed or stalled reads. Consumers that reconcile the artifact against its own metadata (CI diff/gate checks, verify tools comparing `entry-count` to observed row count) see a mismatch and reject a file this generator considers valid. The previous behaviour was internally consistent (`entries.map` at base line 20 over the same `entries.length`), so this is a regression introduced by this diff, not a pre-existing issue.

findings.title: entry-count header no longer matches rows after stale filtering
findings.whyItBreaks: The only change to the emitted artifact is that stale entries are dropped from the body (line 20-21 now maps over `live`), while line 22 still passes `entries.length` to `headerLines`, which formats it as `# entry-count:` (src/manifest.ts:15). Before this PR, `entry-count` always equaled the number of rows; after it, the header overstates the row count by exactly the number of stale entries (e.g. entries=[a(stale),b(live)] emits `# entry-count: 2` with 1 row; all-stale input emits `# entry-count: N` with 0 rows). Any consumer of this persisted manifest that trusts the header — integrity check `rows == entry-count`, pre-sizing a parse loop, or diffing counts across runs — now sees a mismatch/phantom entries and either rejects a valid manifest or reads a truncated/over-allocated set. The stale entries also vanish with no trace, so a reader cannot tell 'dropped as stale' from 'file deleted'.

findings.title: Normalize stored_hash before hmac.compare_digest in check()
findings.whyItBreaks: hmac.compare_digest only accepts two bytes-like values or two ASCII-only str values; anything else raises TypeError. token_hash() returns an ASCII hex str, but stored_hash comes from the caller/persistence layer. Before this change, a None (unprovisioned/missing column) or bytes (raw .digest()) stored_hash made `token_hash(...) == stored_hash` return False, so guard() at app/token.py:13-16 produced a clean 401. After the change the same inputs raise TypeError, which guard() does not catch, so a normal client token submission becomes an unhandled 500 on the request path instead of an authentication rejection.

findings.title: Restore execute() behavior instead of unconditional throw
findings.whyItBreaks: The body was replaced by `throw new Error("always fails")`, so the public export `execute(input: string): string` fails for 100% of inputs and can never produce its declared return value. The previous implementation (base b9f0752) returned `input.toUpperCase()`; every consumer of this exported symbol now gets an uncaught exception instead of a result, and the failure message carries no caller/input context to triage. The unchanged signature `: string` (line 1) still promises a returned string, so callers that trust the contract (and any that only catch to log-and-continue) will treat a guaranteed failure as a normal path. There is no input, flag, or fallback under which this function works, so this is not a conditional regression — it is a dead core path shipped as a working API.

findings.title: Exported execute() now throws unconditionally, removing uppercase behavior
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation returned input.toUpperCase(); head replaces the body with `throw new Error("always fails")`. execute is `export`ed with signature `(input: string) => string`, so the declared contract promises a string result, but the body computes nothing and no return statement is reachable — the `string` return type is a lie. Any consumer that previously got a deterministic transformed string now gets an uncaught exception on the ordinary (non-error) path, i.e. the module's one core capability is unusable. The `input` parameter is also now dead, so even a partial/stub interpretation is impossible: there is no input for which the call succeeds. This is not error handling (no new error condition is detected), it is the removal of working behavior behind a throwaway placeholder, and it regresses every existing caller on upgrade.

findings.title: Restore execute() return value; it now throws for every input
findings.whyItBreaks: The public signature still declares `(input: string): string`, but the body is now an unconditional `throw new Error("always fails")` with no reachable return. Every call site of the module's only export gets an exception instead of the uppercased string it previously always received — the function is 100% unusable for all inputs, the TypeScript return type is now a lie, and any caller that does not add a try/catch crashes at runtime. Nothing in the repo (no tests, no guards, no feature flag, no error-type change) indicates a deliberate contract change; the parameter `input` is also now silently ignored.

findings.title: isEligible viewer check blocks handle()'s read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: handle() is the only consumer of isEligible. Line 24 short-circuits to "rejected" whenever isEligible returns false, so the new `if (req.role === "viewer") return false;` at line 18 makes the `if (req.role === "viewer") return "read-only";` branch at line 25 unreachable for every input (status/role/attempts are the only fields, and the viewer check precedes it). Base behavior (git show b6649db:src/handler.ts) returned "read-only" for {status:"active", role:"viewer", attempts<5}; after this change the same request returns "rejected". Viewers lose the read-only capability that the same function explicitly still implements, and isEligible is exported, so any external caller that gated a read-only affordance on it silently loses it too. Admin/editor paths are unchanged.

findings.title: Do not gate read-only access with isEligible's new viewer check
findings.whyItBreaks: isEligible is the single "may proceed" gate read by handle at src/handler.ts:24, and handle still implements a distinct viewer outcome at src/handler.ts:25 ("read-only"). Adding `req.role === "viewer"` to the gate means every active viewer with attempts < MAX_ATTEMPTS — previously routed to "read-only" — now short-circuits to "rejected", and the viewer branch at line 25 becomes unreachable dead code (the same condition is now tested twice, once where it can never be true). So one shared predicate silently blocks a second, independently approvable action: read-only access for viewers. Callers of the exported isEligible also get a changed contract (eligibility no longer means "processable status/attempts", it now embeds an authorization rule) with no update to handle or the Role docs. If the intent really is that viewers must be hard-rejected, then the diff is incomplete (dead branch left behind); if read-only access is intended, the diff is a user-facing regression for an entire role.

findings.title: Remove viewer rejection from isEligible or serve read-only before it
findings.whyItBreaks: isEligible is the single gate used by handle() at src/handler.ts:24, and it is evaluated BEFORE the role routing. With the added `if (req.role === "viewer") return false;`, every viewer (status active, attempts < MAX_ATTEMPTS) now hits `return "rejected"` at line 24, so line 25 `if (req.role === "viewer") return "read-only";` is dead code. At base (304e935:src/handler.ts:14-18) isEligible did not inspect role, so that same viewer returned "read-only". The shared eligibility predicate therefore blocks a distinct, legitimately-approvable action (read-only serving for viewers), not just the write/mutate paths it was meant to gate; callers of the exported isEligible also lose the ability to distinguish "ineligible for handling" from "read-only only".

findings.title: Payment check added to canProceed also blocks saveDraft
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is one shared predicate with two distinct call-sites: submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). Adding `order.payment === "paid"` tightens both. For the ordinary draft state {state:"draft", payment:"missing"} the base returned true (saveDraft -> "saved"); the head returns false, so saveDraft now returns "blocked". A user can no longer persist an in-progress draft until payment exists — an action that is legitimately approvable independent of this gate's payment concern, and a dead-end for exactly the order shape a draft normally has (payment is expected to be filled in later). submitOrder is the only action payment genuinely gates.

findings.title: Split submit gate from draft-save gate in canProceed
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is read by two distinct actions: submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). At base the predicate was `order.state !== "ready"`, so {state:"draft", payment:"missing"} returned true and saveDraft returned "saved". With the new `&& order.payment === "paid"` (src/policy.ts:7) that same order now returns false, so saveDraft returns "blocked" (src/actions.ts:9-10): a user with an unpaid draft can no longer persist their work — the only behavior row that changed is silently repurposed from a submit precondition into a write precondition, and the payment check has no bearing on whether a draft may be saved (drafts exist precisely before payment).

findings.title: Do not gate saveDraft on payment; unpaid drafts now blocked
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is the single shared predicate behind both submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). Adding `order.payment === "paid"` means an order with {state:"draft", payment:"missing"} — the normal state of a work-in-progress, pre-payment draft — now evaluates to `true && false` = false, so saveDraft() returns "blocked" instead of "saved". Base behavior (src/policy.ts:7 @ c51a4f7) returned true for that input, so this diff drops every unpaid draft write. Payment is a precondition of submitting, not of saving a draft, so the new clause over-blocks an action it does not legitimately govern. The only surviving pass-through input is {state:"draft", payment:"paid"}.

findings.title: Publish snapshot mixes two refs: commit from channel, files from stable
findings.whyItBreaks: The `Snapshot` contract pairs `commit`, `channel` and `files` as one consistent view of a single commit (base version resolved files from `head`). After this change, `commit` is still `repo.headCommit(channel)` (line 13/16) and `channel` is still the caller's argument (line 17), but `files` is now `repo.filesAt(stable)` where `stable = repo.headCommit("stable")` (lines 14, 18). For every channel other than `stable` — including `DEFAULT_CHANNEL = "main"` (src/channels.ts:1) — the returned snapshot advertises commit X while carrying the file manifest of an unrelated, older/diverged commit. Any consumer that publishes, serves, verifies or GCs based on `snapshot.files` while recording `snapshot.commit` writes the wrong payload for the channel (and the commit↔files pairing can no longer be validated by anyone downstream). The added unconditional `headCommit("stable")` lookup also makes every publish, including for channels that never touch `stable`, depend on a `stable` ref existing. If the intent really is 'publish stable content', the only self-consistent shape is commit=stable/channel="stable"; if the intent is 'publish this channel's snapshot', files must come from `head` as before.

findings.title: Snapshot files come from 'stable' while commit reports channel HEAD
findings.whyItBreaks: The Snapshot struct pairs `commit` with `files`; before this change both were derived from the same value (`head = repo.headCommit(channel)` -> `repo.filesAt(head)`). After the change, line 13 still resolves HEAD for the requested channel and line 16 publishes it as `commit`, but line 18 hands back the tree of a different, hardcoded ref: `repo.headCommit("stable")`. For any channel other than `stable` (e.g. DEFAULT_CHANNEL = "main", src/channels.ts:1) the caller receives a file set belonging to another branch — stale or foreign content — while the accompanying `commit` claims it is the channel HEAD, so provenance checks, caching keyed on `commit`, and diff/verification against `commit` all silently agree with the wrong data. The 'stable' ref is also never validated by `isValidChannel` and may not exist, adding a lookup failure on every publish regardless of channel. Nothing in the repo consumes the new shape (only these two source files exist), so the mismatch is not masked by a compensating caller.

findings.title: publishSnapshot reads files from hard-coded "stable", not channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: Lines 13/16 resolve and report `commit = repo.headCommit(channel)`, but line 18 now calls `repo.filesAt(stable)` where `stable` is `repo.headCommit("stable")` (line 14) — a ref unrelated to the `channel` argument. For any channel other than "stable" (including DEFAULT_CHANNEL "main", src/channels.ts:1), the returned Snapshot advertises one commit while carrying another ref's file list, so the published snapshot content is silently the wrong tree (stale or foreign files) for the named commit/channel. The `stable` lookup is also performed unconditionally on every call, even when `channel === "stable"`, so a repo/Remote without a `stable` ref makes `headCommit("stable")` fail (or return an empty/unknown commit) for publishes of unrelated channels. Base (ce2d548) used `repo.filesAt(head)`, which was self-consistent.

findings.title: Honor new limit parameter in build() instead of hardcoding max_count
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff adds `limit=10` to the public signature but never reads it: line 2 still sets `max_count = 10` and line 4 iterates `range(max_count)`, so `build("x", limit=1)` (or `limit=0`, `limit=100`) returns 10 entries regardless. Any caller that passes a limit to cap output size, pagination, or a payload/quota bound silently receives 10 records and cannot distinguish "capped" from "not capped" — the returned data is wrong, not merely unoptimized. The parameter's default (10) coincidentally matches the hardcoded value, which hides the defect from existing tests. There are no in-repo callers (rg for `build(` finds only the definition), so this ships as a broken public contract rather than a caught error.

findings.title: Remove dead `limit` param or actually apply it in build()
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 1 adds the public parameter `limit=10`, which promises callers that the returned list is capped at `limit` items. The body implements none of it: line 2 still hardcodes `max_count = 10` and line 4 iterates `range(max_count)`, never reading `limit`. So `build("a", limit=3)` returns 10 items (caller's cap silently ignored — over-production, e.g. a paginated/bounded consumer emits 10 rows where it sized for 3) and `build("a", limit=100)` returns 10 items (caller's request silently truncated). Because `limit` defaults to 10 — identical to the old hardcoded value — existing calls behave unchanged, which hides the defect: it only surfaces for the exact calls the new parameter exists to serve, and the caller gets no error, only wrong data. It also introduces two sources of truth for the same cap (`limit` vs `max_count`), which will drift on the next edit.

findings.title: Make build() honor its new limit parameter instead of ignoring it
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff adds `limit=10` to the public signature, which advertises that the caller controls how many items are returned, but `max_count = 10` (line 2) is still a hardcoded constant and `limit` is never referenced anywhere in the function body. Any caller doing `build('x', limit=3)` receives 10 entries; `build('x', limit=1000)` receives 10. The result data a caller receives is unaffected by the parameter, so truncation/sizing intent silently mis-fires (caller gets 3.3x the requested items, or cannot get more than 10) with no error and no way to distinguish it from a working cap.

findings.title: Rename promises positivity validation the body does not perform
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed carrier `parse_positive_int` promises a positive, validated integer, but the body is still a bare `int(value)` cast (src/validators.py:2) with no positivity or type check. The one in-repo caller `charge` (src/validators.py:6-7) relies on that promise and multiplies the value straight through, so `charge('-5')` returns -500 and `total_cents(['-5'])` returns -500 — a negative/zero amount is silently accepted and flows into the money value callers return, instead of being rejected as the name advertises. Callers outside this module will trust the name rather than read the body.

findings.title: parse_positive_int promises positivity but performs no validation
findings.whyItBreaks: The rename read_int -> parse_positive_int encodes a validation promise in the public symbol name, while the body is byte-for-byte the unchanged int(value) (src/validators.py:2). Substituting values the name forbids: parse_positive_int(-5) -> -5, parse_positive_int(0) -> 0, parse_positive_int("-1") -> -1 — nothing is rejected. The only in-module consumer, charge() (src/validators.py:5-7), feeds that unchecked value straight into n * 100, so charge(-5) returns -500 and charge(0) returns 0; total_cents() then sums the negatives into an overall credit with no error path. Previously the neutral name read_int promised nothing, so no caller could be trusting validation that does not exist; after this rename every caller reading the contract skips its own positivity guard, and a bad sign becomes a silently wrong monetary amount instead of a rejected input. There is no doc/type/raise in the file backing the promised behavior, so the defect ships with the rename itself.

findings.title: Make parse_positive_int actually reject non-positive values
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed carrier promises a positive int, but the body is unchanged `return int(value)`, which accepts 0 and negatives (parse_positive_int(-100) -> -100, parse_positive_int(True) -> 1, and it still truncates floats). Its only in-file consumer, charge() at line 6-7, multiplies that value by 100, and total_cents() at line 10-11 sums it, so a signed amount silently produces a negative charge and a reduced/negative total instead of an error. Because parse_positive_int is a module-level (importable) helper, the name itself is the contract: callers will reasonably drop their own positivity check on the strength of it, and the diff introduces a validation promise with zero validation behind it — the worst case for a money path.

findings.title: Restore defensive copy: apply_values now mutates caller's df
findings.whyItBreaks: Base behavior (12ea121:src/transform.py:5-8) was `result = df.copy()` ... `return result`: the input frame was never touched and the returned frame was a distinct object. Head deletes the copy and writes through `df.loc[...]` on the caller's object, so `apply_values(df, m)` returns the *same* object it was passed (`out is df`) and has already modified the caller's `df`. Concrete wrong behaviors introduced: (a) a caller that keeps using its original frame after the call — baseline/before-after comparison, retry with a different mapping, applying a second independent mapping — now sees already-overwritten `value` cells, i.e. silently wrong data, not an error; (b) `a = apply_values(df, m1); b = apply_values(df, m2)` no longer yields two independent results, `a is b is df` and `a` contains m2's updates (accumulating, non-reversible); (c) the write now lands on whatever the caller handed in, so if that frame is itself a slice/view of a larger frame the assignment propagates into the parent (SettingWithCopyWarning path, and a raise under pandas' ChainedAssignmentError semantics) — the exact case `.copy()` guaranteed against. The name, signature and return statement are unchanged, so nothing signals the new aliasing/in-place semantics to existing callers.

findings.title: Restore defensive copy: apply_values now mutates caller's DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: Base did `result = df.copy()` and wrote/returned `result`; head writes through `df.loc[...]` (line 6) and returns `df` (line 7). The returned object is now identical to the argument (`ret is df`), so every caller loses its input data as a side effect of calling a function whose shape ("transform values, return a frame") implies a produced result. Concretely: `out = apply_values(df, m)` silently changes `df`, so any subsequent read of `df` (logging the pre-transform state, applying a second mapping, retry after a partial failure, or reusing one cached frame across requests) sees the overwritten values; where the mapping key is absent, `ret.loc[...]` already failed on the caller's own frame instead of a scratch copy. The removed copy also changes the write target from an owned frame to a possibly non-owned one: if the caller passes a slice/view (`df[df.x > 0]`), `df.loc[...]` on line 6 can raise/warn under pandas' set-with-copy / CoW rules, turning a previously safe call into an error or a dropped write. Nothing else in the repo calls `apply_values` (only its own definition at src/transform.py:4), so this is not mitigated by an in-repo in-place consumer.

findings.title: Restore defensive copy in apply_values (stops mutating caller df)
findings.whyItBreaks: Base assigned into `result = df.copy()` (base src/transform.py:5-8) and returned that copy; head writes `df.loc[...] = value` (src/transform.py:6) and returns the same object (src/transform.py:7). So `out = apply_values(df, mapping)` now aliases the input: the caller's original DataFrame is silently overwritten, any baseline comparison of df vs out is trivially equal, and two successive calls with different mappings on the same frame accumulate into it (the second call's `df["key"] == key` predicate at line 6 reads rows the first call already rewrote), producing wrong/merged output rather than two independent transforms. The only in-file contract carriers are unchanged (`def apply_values(df, mapping)` returning a transformed frame), so callers legitimately rely on non-mutation; nothing in the repo was updated or tested for the new side effect (no tests exist).

findings.title: Restore CI workflow at .github/workflows/ci.yml; move to docs/ disables it
findings.whyItBreaks: The rename is content-identical (similarity 100%) but changes the only path GitHub Actions honors. After this change the head tree contains no .github/workflows/* file at all (verified via git ls-tree -r af0ec63), so the `on: push` / `on: pull_request` trigger no longer exists and `npm ci`, `npm run lint`, `npm test` never execute on any push or PR. Unlinted, untested code can now merge with a green (absent) checks tab, and the unchanged README.md:5 still advertises "CI runs lint and tests on every push" — the promise is now false, so reviewers/consumers rely on a guardrail that silently no longer exists. docs/ci.md itself is inert YAML-as-markdown: as documentation it is also wrong (no such workflow runs).

findings.title: Restore CI workflow; do not move .github/workflows/ci.yml to docs
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub only executes workflows found under .github/workflows/. After this rename that directory no longer exists in head (git ls-tree -r HEAD shows only .needlefish/answers.json, README.md, docs/ci.md, src/index.ts; .github/ is absent), so the `ci` pipeline (checkout -> npm ci -> npm run lint -> npm test) stops running entirely on pushes and PRs. The renamed content is unchanged YAML (similarity index 100%) — it is not documentation, so docs/ci.md is inert and never executes. Net effect: every commit merges and ships with zero automated lint/test enforcement, and the failure is silent (no red X, just no check), so regressions in src/index.ts reach main unnoticed. README.md:5 still asserts "CI runs lint and tests on every push", which is now false, so reviewers/consumers will keep trusting a safety net that no longer exists.

findings.title: Restore CI workflow: rename to docs/ci.md disables lint/test runs
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub only discovers and executes workflow files under .github/workflows/. The 100%-similarity rename takes the identical `name: ci` / `on: push, pull_request` definition out of that directory and into docs/ci.md, so after this merge no workflow exists at all: `npm run lint` and `npm test` never run on push or PR. The file is still valid GitHub Actions YAML (lines 1-12), not Markdown, so it is not even usable as documentation — it is a disabled pipeline parked in docs/. Every subsequent commit merges unverified, and README.md:5 ('CI runs lint and tests on every push.') is now a false promise that readers and branch-protection checks rely on.

findings.title: Make parse_positive_int actually reject non-positive input
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed public carrier promises "positive int", but the body is unchanged `s.parse().unwrap_or(0)`: "-5" parses to -5 and "abc"/"" collapse to 0. The only consumer, `charge` (src/parse.rs:6-7), multiplies the returned value straight by 100 with no positivity guard, so `charge("-5")` returns -500 (an inverted/negative charge) and `charge("1e9")` or `charge("")` returns 0. Because the name now asserts validation, callers reasonably stop re-checking the result, and the returned 0 is indistinguishable between "legitimate zero", "invalid text" and "unparseable", so a billing failure is silently reported as a real zero-amount charge.

findings.title: parse_positive_int promises positivity but returns negatives
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed public carrier (was `read_int` @ base src/parse.rs:1) states the result is a positive int, but the unchanged body computes `s.parse().unwrap_or(0)` (src/parse.rs:2): `-5` parses successfully and is returned as `-5`, no sign check, clamp, or rejection exists. The only caller in the repo relies on that promise — `charge` (src/parse.rs:6) feeds the value straight into `n * 100` (src/parse.rs:7), so `charge("-5")` returns `-500`, i.e. a negative amount on a path named/typed as a charge, with no way for callers to distinguish a rejected/duplicate/negative amount from a legitimate one (parse failure is also folded into the legitimate value `0`). Because the carrier is `pub`, the name itself is the contract for external users of this module, so this is a present defect, not a hypothetical.

findings.title: parse_positive_int does not enforce positivity; charge yields negative amounts
findings.whyItBreaks: The public name was changed from `read_int` to `parse_positive_int`, which promises a validated positive integer, but the body is unchanged: `s.parse().unwrap_or(0)` accepts any parseable i64, including negatives and zero ("-50" -> -50, "0" -> 0) and maps every malformed input to 0. Callers therefore cannot distinguish "invalid", "zero" and "negative" from a legitimate positive value. The relying caller `charge` at src/parse.rs:6-7 multiplies the return by 100 with no guard, so `charge("-50")` returns -5000 — a signed (refund-shaped) amount produced from unvalidated caller input — and `charge("abc")` silently returns 0 instead of surfacing the failure. Because the carrier is `pub`, the name itself is the contract; the rename asserts validation that does not exist.

findings.title: Remove or borrow dbg! call that moves `items` and breaks build
findings.whyItBreaks: std's `dbg!` expands to `match $val { tmp => { eprintln!(...); tmp } }`, i.e. it takes the expression BY VALUE and moves it. `items: Vec<String>` is not `Copy`, so `dbg!(items);` moves the parameter into the statement (the returned `tmp` temporary is dropped at the semicolon) and the very next line `let total = items.len();` (src/store.rs:3) reads the moved local. rustc rejects this with E0382 ("use of moved value: `items`"), so `src/store.rs` fails to compile and `process` — the only public symbol in the file, and the path the rest of the change set depends on — becomes unusable. Verified there is no user-defined `dbg!` macro shadowing std's (only one .rs file in the tree, `grep -rn dbg` hits just this line), so the by-value move semantics apply unchanged. Secondary issue with the same line: even once borrowed, `dbg!` prints the full `Vec<String>` payload of every call to stderr on a public path, which is debug leftover, not intended behavior.

findings.title: Remove dbg! that moves `items`, breaking compilation of process()
findings.whyItBreaks: std's `dbg!` expands to `match $val { tmp => { ...; tmp } }`, i.e. it takes ownership of its argument and only avoids a move when given a reference or a `Copy` value. `items: Vec<String>` is neither, so line 2 moves `items` into the macro's temporary; line 3 (`let total = items.len();`) then borrows a moved value and the whole crate fails to compile with E0382 (`borrow of moved value: items`). Since `process` is a `pub fn` (the crate's only public entry point, src/store.rs:1), nothing built on this crate can compile — this is a hard build break, not a cosmetic debug leftover. Secondary defect even if the move were avoided: `dbg!` writes the full `Vec<String>` contents to stderr from a library function, unconditionally and unfilterable, which is also leaking caller data into logs.

findings.title: Remove debug leftover: dbg!(items) moves items, crate fails to compile
findings.whyItBreaks: std::dbg takes its argument by value and returns it; the `;` discards the returned value, so `items: Vec<String>` (not Copy) is moved out on line 2. Line 3 `items.len()` then borrows a moved value: `error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: items`. Verified with the environment toolchain (rustc 1.75.0) on the exact head body for editions 2015/2018/2021 — all three abort with E0382, while the base body compiles cleanly. This is a hard build break of the only public entry point (`pub fn process`), so any crate/user depending on src/store.rs stops building; it is also a debug leftover that would spam stderr from a library function on every call if it were made to compile.

findings.title: changedPaths computed against 'latest' but labelled from pinned revision
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset interface (src/changeset.ts:7-8) promises 'Revision the changed paths were computed against. Consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision.' Line 17 still sets fromRevision to store.resolve(pinnedTag), but line 18 now passes store.resolve("latest") to readChangedPaths. Whenever the pin lags head (the normal reason a pin exists), the two revisions differ, so the returned path set is the diff from a newer base while the consumer replays it onto the pinned base: files changed between pinned and latest are treated as already present (skipped/incomplete update, stale content kept), and files whose paths only exist post-latest can be replayed against a revision that does not contain them. Before this diff both values came from the same `from` variable, so the pair was always self-consistent. A caller cannot detect the mismatch from the returned object.

findings.title: changedPaths computed against 'latest' while fromRevision is pinned
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset doc comment (src/changeset.ts:7-10, unchanged carrier) promises fromRevision is 'Revision the changed paths were computed against. Consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision.' After this diff, line 15 resolves a second, different revision (`latest`) and line 18 feeds it to readChangedPaths, while line 17 still reports fromRevision = resolve(pinnedTag). Whenever latest != pinnedTag (the normal case for a pinned consumer), the returned changedPaths describe a diff against a baseline the changeset does not name: replaying them on top of fromRevision applies paths that did not change relative to that revision and omits paths that did — silently wrong/missing results, and the caller has no signal because both fields are non-empty strings. This is a public exported function, so the broken pairing ships to every consumer immediately; no caller can reconcile it after the fact.

findings.title: changedPaths computed against `latest` but tagged with pinned fromRevision
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset contract (src/changeset.ts:6-9) states fromRevision is "the revision the changed paths were computed against" and that "consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision." Base did `store.readChangedPaths(from)`; head passes `latest` (src/changeset.ts:18) while fromRevision stays `from` (src/changeset.ts:17). `readChangedPaths`'s parameter is itself named `fromRevision` (src/changeset.ts:3), i.e. the diff base. So the returned pair is internally inconsistent: the path set describes "what changed since latest", not "what changed since the pinned revision". Every change between `pinnedTag` and `latest` is dropped from changedPaths (consumer never replays it → silently missing changes on the pinned target), and any path that only changed after `latest`'s predecessor is replayed onto a base that lacks its prerequisite state. `from` is now dead except as a label, and `store.resolve("latest")` adds a second, unrelated resolution that can also fail the whole call for deployments whose store has no `latest` tag.

findings.title: Update src/query.sql for users.email -> contact_email rename
findings.whyItBreaks: The rename removes the column `email` from `users`, but src/query.sql:1 still reads `SELECT email FROM users;`. After this migration is applied, that stored query fails outright (SQLite/PostgreSQL: `no such column: email` / `column "email" does not exist`), so every path that executes src/query.sql is broken — not just degraded. The rename shipped without its call-site: `rg -n email` over the head tree shows the only remaining reference is src/query.sql:1.

findings.title: Update users.email readers before renaming the column
findings.whyItBreaks: The rename leaves `users.email` nonexistent, but src/query.sql:1 still does `SELECT email FROM users;`. Any deployment that runs 0002 while the old query is live fails outright on every read of that path (SQLite: `no such column: email`; Postgres: `column "email" does not exist`; MySQL: `Unknown column 'email'`) — the stored data is intact but unreachable through the shipped query, so this is a broken core read path on upgrade, not a cosmetic rename.

findings.title: Update src/query.sql to contact_email before shipping the rename
findings.whyItBreaks: 0001_init.sql:1 adds users.email and this new migration renames that column to contact_email, so after 0002 is applied the column `email` no longer exists. `git grep -w email HEAD` shows exactly one live reader of that column in the repo: src/query.sql:1 `SELECT email FROM users;`, which is unchanged by this diff. Every execution of that query post-migration fails outright (SQLite: `no such column: email`; Postgres: `column "email" does not exist`) — this is a hard break of an existing read path, not a stale-name cleanup, and it is not fixable after deploy without another migration.

findings.title: Build users(email) index without locking out table writes
findings.whyItBreaks: migrations/0001_init.sql:1 uses SERIAL, i.e. this is Postgres. Plain CREATE INDEX takes a SHARE lock on users for the whole build, which blocks every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (signups, profile/email updates) while allowing reads. Applied to a populated users table during an ordinary deploy, the migration stalls until writes drain and queued write transactions pile up behind it; the longer the build, the longer the write outage. No precondition in this repo (no runner config, no downtime/maintenance flag) proves the target table is empty or the deploy is offline, so the safe form is not obviously unnecessary.

findings.title: Handle missing settings file in startup() instead of crashing on None
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() explicitly returns None when the path does not exist (app/config.py:6-7), and startup()'s only consumer now does settings["workers"] on that value (app/config.py:14). With the deleted `if settings is None: settings = {"workers": 1, ...}` guard, any run whose config file is absent raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable` at startup — a hard crash on the main entry path where the base version completed successfully. This is an upgrade regression for every existing deployment/developer environment that relied on the optional (absent) settings file, and the traceback names neither the missing path nor the cause. The same applies to a settings file containing JSON `null`, which json.load returns as None.

findings.title: Handle missing config in startup() instead of crashing with TypeError
findings.whyItBreaks: `load_settings` still returns `None` when the file does not exist (app/config.py:6-7, unchanged). With the deleted guard, `startup(path)` now evaluates `None["workers"]` and raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable` at line 14 for any caller passing a path to a not-yet-created config file. Base behaviour for the same input was a successful start with `workers=1`; on upgrade, fresh installs / first-run / deployments whose config has not been written yet go from 'starts with defaults' to 'crashes at startup' with a message that names neither the file nor the cause. `startup` is a public module-level function (no leading underscore), so every existing caller inherits this new crash path.

findings.title: startup() crashes with TypeError when config file is absent
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() (app/config.py:5-9) returns None on two reachable inputs: the path does not exist (`return None`, line 7) and a file whose JSON body is `null` (json.load -> None). The deleted lines were the only guard for that value, so `settings["workers"]` at app/config.py:14 now executes `None["workers"]` and raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable` instead of returning the previous default (workers=1, region=us-east-1). Every existing deployment/first-run/local-dev checkout that starts without a config file — previously a supported path — now dies at startup with an opaque TypeError that does not name the config path, i.e. a crash loop in any supervisor that restarts on failure. The same call also raises TypeError (not KeyError) when the file exists but parses to a non-dict (e.g. `[]`, `"x"`), so no caller can distinguish 'no config supplied' from 'corrupt config'.

findings.title: Charge() swallows gateway error and returns nil on failed charge
findings.whyItBreaks: Base returned fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err) on Submit failure; head replaces that return with log.Printf and falls through to `return nil`. Charge is an exported function whose error return is the only signal of gateway failure, so every caller (and any future caller) now receives the identical result for "charged" and "not charged" — the failure is only visible in a log line the caller cannot inspect or branch on. Callers that record, persist, or report success on a nil error will book/complete a charge that never happened, no retry or fallback path is ever taken, and the wrapped error context (%w) is lost so upstream errors.Is/As matching breaks too. There is no other error channel (no return flag, no callback) that keeps failure distinguishable, so this is not a legitimate log-and-continue contract.

findings.title: Return gateway submit error from Charge instead of logging nil error
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, a Submit failure propagated to the caller as `charge failed: %w` (base pay/charge.go:14-16 in 5223afc). After the change, the failure is only written to the log (pay/charge.go:17) and `Charge` falls through to `return nil` (pay/charge.go:19). `Charge` is an exported function in a payment package: its `error` result is the sole channel distinguishing "money moved" from "gateway rejected the request". Every caller — including any existing `if err := pay.Charge(...); err != nil { retry/refund/mark-charge-failed }` — now takes the success branch on a failed charge, so an uncharged order is recorded/billed/reported as paid, retries and escalation never fire, and the only trace is a log line that no decision point reads. Failure and success become unrepresentable in the return value, which is a present contract defect, not a hypothetical about future callers (per the rule that an exported/public swallow site is a finding even with no in-repo caller). The `%v` formatting also discards the wrapped error chain, so callers that could inspect the cause (errors.Is/As) lose it as well.

findings.title: Restore error propagation in Charge on Submit failure
findings.whyItBreaks: Base returned `fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err)` when gw.Submit failed; the new code only calls log.Printf and falls through to `return nil` (line 19). Charge is an exported function whose contract is its `error` return, so after this change the signature can never signal a submit failure: the error signal is destroyed at line 17 and never reaches any caller (previously_reached = the Charge return at base pay/charge.go:17, now_receives = a bare `nil` at pay/charge.go:19). Any caller doing the standard `if err := pay.Charge(...); err != nil { retry/alert } else { mark order paid / fulfil }` will now take the success branch for a charge that was not submitted, i.e. failure and success become indistinguishable at every decision point — lost charges recorded as collected, no retry, no alert, and the %v formatting also drops the wrapped error chain so the cause is not even recoverable from the log line. Only the cents<=0 validation path still returns an error, which makes the asymmetry worse: callers have a working err==nil-means-succeeded mental model that is now false.

findings.title: Restore tenantId in settings cache key (cross-tenant leak)
findings.whyItBreaks: cacheKey(name) returns `settings:${name}` with no tenant component, and the module-level `cache` Map (line 5) is shared by all callers. First call settingsFor("tenantA","smtp_relay",store) stores tenantA's value under `settings:smtp_relay` (line 16); the next call settingsFor("tenantB","smtp_relay",store) hits line 14 and returns tenantA's value WITHOUT calling store.fetch(tenantB,...) — so tenant B is served tenant A's setting (cross-tenant data disclosure and misrouting, e.g. tenant B's mail/credentials/api keys going to tenant A's endpoint), and tenant B's correct value is never fetched while the entry lives. The `tenantId` parameter on line 11 is still in the signature and is still passed to store.fetch on line 15, so the contract promises per-tenant resolution while the body implements a tenant-agnostic lookup — callers cannot detect this from the return value. Whichever tenant populates the entry first wins for all tenants.

findings.title: Restore tenantId in settings cache key to stop cross-tenant leakage
findings.whyItBreaks: `cache` (src/settings.ts:5) is module-global and shared by all callers, but the new `cacheKey(name)` (src/settings.ts:7-9) keys only on `name`, so `settingsFor("tenantA","smtp_host",store)` writes `settings:smtp_host` and every later call `settingsFor("tenantB","smtp_host",store)` returns tenantA's value from the hit at src/settings.ts:14 without ever calling `store.fetch`. `SettingsStore.fetch(tenantId, name)` (src/settings.ts:2) is explicitly tenant-scoped, so per-tenant values are the normal case: first tenant to read a setting name wins and other tenants silently receive foreign configuration — cross-tenant disclosure of secret/URL-like settings and wrong-config execution (a tenant routed to another tenant's endpoint). Base code keyed `${tenantId}:${name}` and had no such leak.

findings.title: invalidate() must keep its tenantId parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature narrows from `invalidate(tenantId, name)` to `invalidate(name)`. Existing callers passing two arguments now fail to compile, and callers passing a single argument change meaning (their `tenantId`/`name` no longer selects the same entry). More importantly, once the key is fixed to be tenant-scoped, a name-only invalidate can no longer target one tenant's entry: any caller clearing tenant A's setting necessarily clears the shared key for all tenants (or, if keyed per tenant, clears nothing), so a per-tenant settings update either leaves stale tenant values cached or evicts unrelated tenants' entries.

findings.title: Restore tenantId in settings cache key (cross-tenant collision)
findings.whyItBreaks: cache is a module-level Map (line 5) shared by all callers, but the new cacheKey(name) drops tenantId, keying only on `settings:${name}`. `store.fetch(tenantId, name)` (line 15) proves the backing store is tenant-partitioned. Substitute two live tenants: settingsFor("acme","plan",s) fetches acme's value and stores it at key "settings:plan"; the next call settingsFor("globex","plan",s) hits line 13-14 and returns acme's value without ever calling the store — tenant B is silently served tenant A's setting (data disclosure / wrong configuration / wrong billing or feature state), and the value is also persisted into the cache entry used by A's later reads. Before this change base key `${tenantId}:${name}` could not collide.

findings.title: invalidate() lost tenantId, cannot expire one tenant's entry
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature was narrowed from invalidate(tenantId, name) to invalidate(name). Two consequences: (a) existing callers `invalidate(tenantId, name)` fail to compile on upgrade (public API break, not a runtime no-op, but a hard upgrade break); (b) with the tenant key restored per finding 1, a single-name invalidate can only delete one arbitrary key shape, so a per-tenant cache invalidation is no longer expressible — a tenant's setting change either leaves that tenant serving a stale value or forces a wildcard delete that is not implemented (cache.delete on `settings:${name}` will not match `${tenantId}:settings:${name}`, i.e. silent no-op invalidation after finding 1's fix).

findings.title: Fix lost-update/oversell race in async reserve()
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 15 reads `remaining` from the map, line 17 suspends on `await this.store.save(...)`, line 18 writes back `remaining - 1` computed from the value read BEFORE the suspension. Any second reserve(sku) call that starts while the first is awaiting (e.g. `await Promise.all([inv.reserve('X'), inv.reserve('X')])` with stock 1) re-reads `remaining = 1`, passes the `remaining <= 0` guard, persists `save('X', 0)` again, and returns `true` — two successful reservations against one unit, and the persisted count is written from a stale value (lost update: stock 2 with two concurrent reserves ends at 1, not 0). The base version (src/inventory.ts:12-17 at 0750bf3) had no await between read and write, so the guard+decrement could not interleave; this diff introduces the window on a hot path where the guard is exactly the oversell protection. Secondary effect: because line 18's write is unconditional, the last-resuming caller clobbers whatever the map holds, so in-memory stock and the value handed to store.save() can also disagree with each other.

findings.title: Non-atomic reserve: await between stock check and decrement oversells
findings.whyItBreaks: At base (git show c3bcfaa:src/inventory.ts) `reserve` had no yield point, so read-guard-write ran atomically within one event-loop turn. Head reads `remaining` (line 15) and passes the `remaining <= 0` guard (line 16), then yields on `await this.store.save(...)` (line 17) before writing `this.stock.set(sku, remaining - 1)` (line 18). Two concurrent calls for the same SKU (e.g. `await Promise.all([inv.reserve('A'), inv.reserve('A')])` with stock 1) both read remaining=1, both pass the guard, both await, both return true, and both write 0 — one unit is sold twice and the durable store receives the same absolute value `0` from both writers (second save is a lost update, not a decrement). Every concurrent caller path (HTTP/RPC handler per request) now has this interleaving; stock can also drift above the true committed count when saves interleave with different `remaining` snapshots.

findings.title: Reserve check-then-act spans an await, allowing oversell/lost update
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base version reserve() contained no await, so read-guard-write ran as one synchronous, uninterruptible block. The diff inserts `await this.store.save(...)` between the read of `remaining` (line 15) and the write `this.stock.set(...)` (line 18). Two overlapping calls for the same SKU both execute lines 15-16 before either resumes: with stock=1, `reserve('a')` twice via Promise.all gives remaining=1 in both, both pass `remaining <= 0`, both call `store.save('a', 0)` (the second overwrite is a lost write of the first reservation) and both set 0 — two units are handed out from one unit of stock, and the backing store is persisted with the wrong remaining count (0 instead of the correct rejection of the second). Every caller that does not explicitly serialize reserve() per SKU (any web/queue/job handler doing Promise.all or fire-and-forget) hits this; it fails silently — no error, just bad inventory data. The same interleaving applies across the store being the source of truth: the value saved is a stale snapshot captured before the await, not a compare-and-set.

findings.title: Migrate retry.ts caller after backoff() unit change to milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds (min(30_000, 2**attempt*1000) @ src/config/backoff.ts:2), but retry.ts:12 still applies the old seconds->ms conversion: `sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`. sleep() takes ms (@src/jobs/retry.ts:3), so on the first failed attempt the job waits min(30_000,1_000)*1000 = 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 min) instead of 1 s, and from attempt 5 onward min(30_000,32_000)*1000 = 30,000,000 ms (~8.3 h) instead of 30 s. Any retry that legitimately recovers on attempt 1 or 2 now looks like a hung/dead worker: backoff is effectively never reached within any operational deadline, `fn()` is not called again for hours, and `throw lastErr` at line 16 is delayed past any caller patience. poll.ts was migrated (line 4) but this second caller of the same changed function was missed.

findings.title: retry.ts still multiplies ms-based backoff by 1000
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed line makes backoff() return milliseconds (Math.min(30_000, 2**attempt * 1000)), but src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still treats the return value as seconds: `await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`. sleep() is declared in ms (retry.ts:3), so the job-retry delay is now multiplied twice. Substituting real values: attempt 0 sleeps 1_000_000 ms (~16.7 min) instead of 1 s; attempt >= 5 hits the cap and sleeps 30_000_000 ms (~8.3 h) instead of 30 s; a 3-attempt failing job blocks ~1h53m where it used to take 7 s. The only caller that was updated (src/net/poll.ts:4) is correct, so this is a missed call-site, not an intended behavior change — retry effectively wedges for hours and the last error is never surfaced in any realistic window. No test covers retry timing.

findings.title: Update remaining backoff() caller in src/jobs/retry.ts after unit change
