findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds (Math.min(30_000, 2**attempt*1000)), but src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still applies the old seconds contract: `await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`. sleep() takes ms, so each retry delay is inflated 1000x: attempt 0 waits 1_000_000 ms (~16.7 min) instead of 1 s, attempt 1 ~33 min, and every attempt from 4 on waits the capped 30_000_000 ms (~8.33 h) instead of 30 s. A retry loop with, e.g., attempts=6 blocks for ~24 h total and can no longer complete within any realistic job/request lifetime; the error is not swallowed but the retry never effectively happens, so this is a silent stall of the retry path. The diff updated only poll.ts (whose net delay is unchanged, so it is correct), leaving this second caller on the old unit contract. No callers of retry() exist inside this repo, so the regression surfaces in external/binary callers rather than in-repo tests.

findings.title: Return f.Close() error instead of discarding it via defer
findings.whyItBreaks: Base behavior was `return f.Close()` (store/save.go:24 @251a6e8), which propagated close failures on the success path. Head replaces it with `defer f.Close()` (line 13) plus `return w.Flush()` (line 20); the deferred close runs after the return value is fixed, so its error is thrown away. bufio.Writer.Flush only hands bytes to the kernel via write(2); the kernel can still report a failure at close time — NFS close-to-open/deferred-write errors and delayed-allocation ENOSPC/EDQUOT on XFS/ext4 are surfaced by close, not by write. Because Save is the exported persistence entry point of package store and returns nil in exactly those cases, a caller cannot distinguish "saved" from "close failed and the bytes were lost", and will continue to treat truncated/absent content as durable state (silent data loss with a success signal).

findings.title: Return the Close error from Save instead of deferring it away
findings.whyItBreaks: Base behaviour was `return f.Close()` (base store/save.go:24), so a close(2) failure surfaced to the caller. Head replaces it with `defer f.Close()` (line 13) whose error result is discarded, and returns only `w.Flush()` (line 20). close() on a file opened with os.Create is where delayed write failures are reported (ENOSPC/EIO on NFS, FUSE and other async/deferred-error filesystems; bufio's Flush only covers the write syscalls it issues itself). Save is the package's exported persistence entry point: on such a failure it returns nil while the persisted file is short/truncated, so callers log/report success and the caller's own state (and any upstream copy of the lines) is silently lost — 'failed' and 'saved successfully' become indistinguishable, exactly the signal the previous version propagated.

findings.title: page_window drops the last row of every page (end - 1 off-by-one)
findings.whyItBreaks:
_window_bounds returns a HALF-OPEN [start, end) pair (line 20: end = min(start + page_size, row_count)), so the last index in the page is end - 1 and range(start, end) is required. The loop was written as range(start, end - 1), which excludes index end - 1 as well: every full page yields page_size - 1 rows, and a final partial page of exactly 1 row yields 0 rows. Concretely, summarize(['a','b','c','d','e','f','g'], 3) now returns '1. a
2. b
---
4. d
5. e
---
' — rows c, f and g vanish, numbering has gaps (2 → 4) and the last page renders empty, with no error raised. summarize(['a'], 3) returns '' (a non-empty list renders as nothing). Base code used range(start, end) and returned all page_size rows, so this is a regression introduced by this diff, and it is silent: callers relying on len(page_window(...)) == page_size (render_page numbering at line 43, summarize page count at line 49) now see truncated data. render_page does not compensate: it numbers by list offset (page_index * page_size + offset), so it cannot detect or repair the dropped tail row.

findings.title: Fix off-by-one that drops last row of every page
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) pair (line 20: end = min(start + page_size, row_count)), but the loop now iterates range(start, end - 1), so index end-1 is never collected. Base code used range(start, end). Concretely: page_window('abcdefghij', 0, 5) returns rows 0-3 instead of 0-4, so summarize('abcdefghij', 5) renders 8 of 10 rows and rows 5 and 10 vanish with no error; with page_size=1 every page is empty (start == end-1) so summarize(rows, 1) returns only the '---' separators and drops ALL content; the final partial page also loses its last row (e.g. 5 rows / size 3 drops row 5). render_page/summarize inherit the loss (lines 40, 52), and the docstring on line 25 promises 'Rows belonging to page_index'.

findings.title: Fix off-by-one in page_window that drops the last row of each page
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) pair (verified: end = min(start + page_size, row_count) @lib/pagination.py:20), but page_window then iterates range(start, end - 1), i.e. rows[start:end-1]. Every full page returns page_size - 1 rows, so a caller silently loses one row per page: page_window(['a','b','c','d'], 0, 2) -> ['a'] (base returned ['a','b']). Because render_page/summarize are built on page_window, summarize also drops one row per page and, whenever the last page holds exactly one row, emits a completely empty page (rows=10, page_size=3: page_index 3 -> start=9, end=10 -> range(9,9) -> ''), so summarize's output ends with a trailing '---\n' separator and no content. Nothing raises or logs — truncated output is indistinguishable from correct output, and the docstring at line 25 promises 'Rows belonging to page_index'.

findings.title: Fix inverted TTL check in TtlCache.get serving stale entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The comparison was flipped from `<` to `>`. With `age > ttlMs` the entry is returned, so any entry older than the TTL is served as a cache hit permanently and is never deleted (line 21/22 only run for fresh entries) — the Map grows without bound and callers get arbitrarily stale data with no expiry guarantee. Conversely, every entry stored within the TTL now fails the check, is deleted at line 21 and returns null at line 22, so a just-written value can never be read back: `set(k,v); get(k)` returns null. The cache is simultaneously useless (always miss when fresh) and unsafe (never expires when stale).

findings.title: Stop splicing inside forEach in pruneDone; done jobs survive
findings.whyItBreaks: splice() shifts the array while forEach is iterating it. forEach fixes the visit range to the original length and reads each index after the shift, so the element immediately following a removed job is never visited. With jobs=[A(pending), B(done), C(done), D(pending)]: index1 removes B, the array becomes [A,C,D], index2 now yields D, so C (done) is never examined and remains in the result — pruneDone returns [A,C,D]. Any run of two or more adjacent done jobs leaves every second one in the pruned list, so a queue consumer re-runs work already marked done (duplicate side effects, jobs never reaching an empty queue).

findings.title: pruneDone mutates the caller's array (was a pure function)
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version returned a new array from filter(); the new version splices the input in place and returns that same reference, so `pruneDone(jobs) === jobs` and the caller's original list silently loses its done jobs. The signature `pruneDone(jobs: Job[]): Job[]` and the `prune*` naming read as a pure derivation, so any caller that keeps using its own array afterwards (e.g. `const pending = pruneDone(all); render(all)` for a full history, or iterating `all` while `pending` is derived from it) now observes a mutated, shortened list — a lost-write/aliasing regression on an exported API, plus the half-pruned result from the iteration bug is written straight back into the caller's data.

findings.title: Fix inverted TTL comparison: cache serves expired entries, drops fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition gates 'is this entry still within its TTL'. With `Date.now() - entry.storedAt > this.ttlMs`, a freshly written entry (age 0 < ttlMs) falls through to `this.entries.delete(key); return null`, so every cache hit becomes a miss, while an entry older than ttlMs is returned as if valid. Because age only increases, expired entries are served forever and are never evicted, so `TtlCache` degenerates into an unbounded stale store with permanent cache misses for live data.

findings.title: pruneDone misses done jobs after splice shifts the array mid-forEach
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.forEach fixes its upper bound at the array's original length and advances its index monotonically, while `jobs.splice(index, 1)` shifts every later element down by one. The element that moves into the just-removed slot is never visited. Substituted: jobs=[doneA, doneB, pending] → k=0 removes doneA, array becomes [doneB, pending], k=1 visits pending, so doneB is never tested and stays in the result. Same shape for [pending, done, done]: the final done is dropped past the truncation point. Any run of two or more consecutive completed jobs — the normal state of a job queue — leaves done jobs in the returned list, so downstream consumers re-dispatch/re-report work already finished.

findings.title: pruneDone now mutates the caller's array; base returned a new array
findings.whyItBreaks: This is an exported function whose base implementation (`jobs.filter(...)`) left the input untouched and returned a fresh array. The new body splices the caller's array in place and returns that same reference. A caller doing `const pending = pruneDone(allJobs)` and then still using `allJobs` (history, counters, retry reporting, an outer loop over the same array) now sees completed jobs silently erased — and, combined with the skip bug above, sees a half-pruned list — so `allJobs` can no longer be used as the full record. Lost-history writes are unrecoverable for the caller.

findings.title: TtlCache.get TTL comparison is inverted (serves expired, drops fresh)
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard now returns entry.value only when age > ttlMs, i.e. exactly when the entry has expired. Base used `< this.ttlMs`. Concretely: set(k,v) then get(k) at age≈0 → `0 > ttlMs` is false → this.entries.delete(key) + return null, so no entry can ever be read back while still fresh (the cache never hits for its entire valid window). Conversely an entry older than ttlMs is returned on every subsequent read and never deleted, so expired data is served indefinitely and the map never evicts — the TTL contract (fresh value returned, stale value evicted as a miss) is exactly reversed. Boundary also shifts: age == ttlMs is now treated as expired.

findings.title: pruneDone splices while forEach iterates, leaving done jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.forEach captures the range of elements before the first callback, and splice shifts later elements left into already-visited indices. Substituting jobs=[A(done),B(done),C(pending)]: k=0 → A done → splice(0,1) → [B,C]; k=1 now visits C (pending), so B is never examined; k=2 is past the new length and is skipped. Result is [B(done), C] — a done job survives pruning, so the queue keeps re-dispatching/re-reporting completed jobs (and, if the caller then re-prunes or acts on the 'remaining' items, reprocesses finished work). Any run of consecutive done jobs loses every other one; an all-done [A,B] returns [B] instead of []. Second, separate behavior change: the base returned a new array from jobs.filter(), the new code mutates and returns the caller's own array (same reference), so a caller that kept the pre-prune list (e.g. for stats/rendering a full job report) now sees done entries silently removed from it.

findings.title: busiest mutates caller's array by dropping the defensive copy
findings.whyItBreaks: The base copied before sorting ([...rows].sort(...)); head calls rows.sort(...) directly, so a query-shaped public function now reorders the caller's array destructively (descending by amount) as a side effect. Array.prototype.sort is in-place, so any caller that keeps the same array alive — e.g. a list it later renders, iterates in insertion/chronological order, aggregates, re-sorts by another key, or persists — silently observes reordered rows after merely asking "which row is busiest". The signature (busiest(rows: Row[]): Row | null) promises a read, not a mutation, and nothing in the contract warns callers their input is destroyed; a caller that sorted ascending beforehand, or relies on original order downstream, gets wrong output with no error. This is a data-integrity change visible to every existing caller, not a style preference.

findings.title: averageAmount returns NaN for empty rows after guard removal
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` guard turns the empty-input case into 0/0, which JS evaluates to NaN (verified). The declared return type is still `number`, so TypeScript does not flag it, and NaN is contagious: any caller that adds, formats, compares, persists, or bills on the result propagates or stores a non-numeric value instead of getting the previous, defined 0. Worse than a crash, it fails silently — comparisons like `avg > threshold` become false, so a zero-row dataset is silently classified as "below threshold", and toFixed()/JSON round-tripping yields "NaN"/null in reports or stored state.

findings.title: averageAmount returns NaN for empty rows after guard removal
findings.whyItBreaks: Base had `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` (git show 9a582cb:src/stats.ts). With it deleted, `total / rows.length` becomes `0 / 0` for an empty array, so the exported `averageAmount(rows: Row[]): number` now returns NaN while its signature still promises a number. NaN is not an error signal — it propagates silently through arithmetic and comparisons (avg > 0 is false, JSON.stringify serializes it as `null`), so any caller averaging a currently-empty set (new tenant, filtered-out day, pre-ingest dashboard) gets an unusable/blank result instead of the previous 0, and downstream totals built from it become NaN too. This is a silent error-downgrade on an exported path, not a specatable edge case.

findings.title: busiest sorts caller's array in place; defensive copy removed
findings.whyItBreaks: Base computed the ranking on a copy (`const ranked = [...rows].sort(...)`, git show 9a582cb:src/stats.ts). The new body calls `rows.sort(...)` directly, and Array.prototype.sort mutates its receiver, so this read-only-looking query now reorders the caller's array in descending `amount` order as a side effect. The public name/signature promises selection only (non-mutation); callers that keep insertion/chronological order (e.g. render rows after computing the busiest, or call busiest() and then iterate the same array) get silently reordered data, and repeated calls mutate shared state in a way that is order-dependent and hard to trace. The only reason `[0] ?? null` still returns the right row is coincidence — the caller's data is the cost.

findings.title: Restore defensive copy in busiest() to stop mutating caller array
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code sorted a copy ([...rows].sort(...)); head sorts rows.sort(...) in place, so a read-only query named busiest() now reorders the caller's array as a side effect. Any caller that keeps using the same array after the call (original insertion/report order, a React/state-held list, an array cached elsewhere by reference) silently sees its data reordered to descending amount. It also hard-fails where it previously worked: sorting an Object.freeze'd array, a frozen store value, or a Proxy/typed-array-backed list throws TypeError ("Cannot assign to read only property '0'") from inside busiest(), where the copy version never wrote to the input. busiest is an exported public function, so the non-mutating contract is the interface even with no in-repo callers.

findings.title: Restore empty-input guard in averageAmount (now returns NaN)
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` was the only thing making the empty case well-defined. With it gone, rows.reduce(...) is 0 and the return is 0/0 = NaN for an empty (or filtered-to-empty) row set. NaN is undetectable by callers that check for a real value (`if (avg)`, `Number.isFinite` absent, `?? 0` does not catch NaN), so it propagates into downstream arithmetic, toFixed/Intl formatting rendered as "NaN", and into persisted/aggregated reports as a poison value that also makes every subsequent sum that includes it NaN. This is a silent behavior change on an exported function whose signature (`: number`) promises a usable number, and it is the case most likely to be hit in production (no rows for the selected period).

findings.title: Restore numeric descending sort in rankScores (default sort() is lexicographic)
findings.whyItBreaks: scores.sort() with no comparator compares elements as strings by UTF-16 code units, so for [9,100,1000] it yields [100,1000,9] and after reverse() [9,1000,100] — not the numeric-descending order the base version produced with (a,b)=>b-a. topPlayers then reads scores[min(n,len)-1] as the cutoff, which is now an arbitrary value rather than the n-th highest score. Two concrete wrong outputs on the exported path: (a) players scores {a:9,b:100,c:1000}, n=2 → cutoff=scores[1]=1000 → filter keeps only c → topPlayers returns 1 player instead of the top 2 (b dropped); (b) players scores {a:50,b:9,c:100}, n=1 → string sort [100,50,9] → reverse [9,50,100] → cutoff=scores[0]=9 → every player passes the filter, slice(0,1) takes the first in input order → returns a(50) as rank 1 instead of c(100), and formatBoard (src/leaderboard.ts:20) prints "1. a (50)". Negative scores regress the same way ({-1,2,10}, n=2 → cutoff=10 → returns only 10). The failure is silent: the result is a well-formed, plausible-looking board.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator in rankScores sort
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator coerces elements to strings and compares them lexicographically, so the base's `scores.sort((a, b) => b - a)` (true numeric descending) is replaced by an order that is wrong for any mixed digit counts (or negatives). topPlayers depends on this order to pick its cutoff at line 15 (`scores[min(n,len)-1]`), so the exported API misbehaves: (a) wrong winner — players=[{nine,9},{ten,10}], n=1 → sort()=[10,9] ("10"<"9") → reverse()=[9,10] → cutoff=9 → filter keeps both → slice(0,1) returns the 9-point player and formatBoard prints "1. nine (9)"; (b) truncated board — players=[{1000},{999},{5000}], n=2 → sort()=[1000,5000,999] → reverse()=[999,5000,1000] → cutoff=scores[1]=5000 → only the 5000 player passes → 1 row returned for a requested top-2, silently dropping a legitimately qualifying player. The same skew mis-orders ranks 2..n (e.g. 9 before 10) whenever scores cross a digit boundary, which is the normal case for leaderboards.

findings.title: rankScores sorts numbers lexicographically, breaking top-N cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: scores.sort() with no comparator converts elements to strings and orders them by UTF-16 code units, then .reverse() flips that order — it is NOT a descending numeric sort. For any player set mixing digit lengths (the normal case for scores), index k of the returned array is no longer the k-th largest score, so `cutoff = scores[Math.min(n, scores.length) - 1]` at line 15 reads a bogus threshold and line 16's filter/slice returns the wrong players. Substituted with real code paths: players [A=3, B=30, C=100, D=200, E=45], n=2. Base (head~): [3,30,100,200,45] -> desc [200,100,45,30,3] -> cutoff=scores[1]=100 -> topPlayers=[C(100),D(200)]. Head: sort() gives [100,200,3,30,45], reverse() gives [45,30,3,200,100] -> cutoff=scores[1]=30 -> filter keeps B,C,D,E -> slice(0,2) returns [B(30),C(100)]. The top scorer D(200) is silently dropped and a 30-point player is returned as #1, which formatBoard (line 19-22) renders directly to the user. The previous comparator `(a, b) => b - a` was the correct implementation and this diff removed it; equivalence only holds by luck when all scores share the same digit count.

findings.title: Restore constant-time compare in HMAC signature verify
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() is the authorization gate for the webhook: handle() (app/webhook.py:14-17) runs the untrusted processor and returns 200 only when verify() is true. Base (935eed3) compared the expected HMAC against the attacker-supplied signature with hmac.compare_digest (constant-time). Head uses Python `==` on str, which short-circuits at the first differing byte, so the comparison latency grows with the number of leading bytes of the supplied signature that match the true HMAC (hex, 64 chars / 128 bits of effective entropy reduced to per-byte guessing). An attacker who can issue repeated requests with forged signatures can measure response timing to fix the signature byte-by-byte (~16*64 guesses instead of 2^128) and forge a signature that passes verify() — i.e. unauthenticated execution of processor(payload) and a 200 response. This is not a style change: it removes the deliberate security property the base line existed to provide, and there is no test in the repo that would catch it (git ls-tree shows only app/webhook.py).

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() is the sole authorization gate for handle(): app/webhook.py:14 returns 401 unless verify() is true, otherwise it runs processor(payload) and returns 200. Base used hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature); head uses `signature_of(...) == given_signature`. Python's `==` on str short-circuits at the first differing character, so the comparison time leaks the length of the matching HMAC prefix. `handle` is a public network-facing entry point that performs exactly one comparison per request and retries freely with a new candidate, so the per-request signal is only weakened, not removed, by network jitter: an attacker who knows the secret-less format (hexdigest of HMAC-SHA256, fixed 64 ASCII hex chars per app/webhook.py:5-6) can drive the forged-signature path and progressively recover a valid signature, then submit payloads the processor executes as if authenticated. The base explicitly used the constant-time primitive for this purpose; reverting to `==` is a security regression, not a simplification. A second behavior change on the same line: compare_digest raises TypeError on mixed bytes/str arguments (loud failure), while `==` returns False, so a caller passing a bytes signature from the framework now gets a permanent silent 401 instead of an error.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: Python's == on str short-circuits at the first differing character, so verification time leaks how many leading bytes of the attacker-supplied value match the expected HMAC. verify() gates the only auth decision in this module (handle() at app/webhook.py:14 returns 401 vs. running processor() on 200), so a remote caller who can issue many webhook requests with an attacker-chosen signature can mount the classic byte-at-a-time HMAC timing oracle (CWE-208) to forge a valid signature without knowing `secret`, bypassing the 401 gate and executing processor() on arbitrary payloads. The removed call was the mitigation, and no other guard in the file compensates. Secondary effect of the same line: because compare_digest rejected mixed str/bytes with TypeError while == silently yields False, a bytes-typed signature from a transport layer now produces a plain 401 instead of a loud error (behavior change, not the main defect).

findings.title: Restore atomicity: apply balances inside the same transaction as ledger
findings.whyItBreaks: The refactor moved _apply_balances() out of the `with db.transaction():` block (line 24 now runs after the context manager has committed line 23). Base had INSERT ledger + both balance UPDATEs in one transaction. Now the ledger row is durably committed before the balance mutations even start, so: (a) if _apply_balances raises (connection lost, constraint, disk full) the ledger already records a transfer that never affected balances — a committed, non-rollbackable inconsistency; (b) the two UPDATEs themselves are no longer atomic with each other, so a failure between line 9 and line 13 debits from_acct without crediting to_acct, destroying money with no rollback path and no error trace distinguishing it from a legitimate balance; (c) any concurrent reader sees a committed ledger entry against stale balances. This is a financial-integrity regression on the core transfer path, not a stylistic change.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside db.transaction() in transfer()
findings.whyItBreaks: Before the diff, the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs were in one `with db.transaction():` block, so any failure rolled the whole transfer back. In the head version only `_record_ledger(...)` (line 23) runs inside the transaction; `_apply_balances(...)` (line 24) runs after the `with` block has committed. Two concrete money-losing states become reachable: (1) the transaction commits the ledger row and then any failure in `_apply_balances` (DB error, constraint/disk failure, dropped connection, process crash) leaves the ledger recording a completed transfer while neither account balance changed — ledger and balances permanently diverge and the error path gives the caller no way to reconcile, since the durable record already says the transfer succeeded. (2) Inside `_apply_balances` (lines 9-16) the debit and the credit are themselves two separate autocommitted statements outside any transaction, so a failure between them debits `from_acct` without crediting `to_acct` — funds are destroyed, and re-running the transfer does not recover them (it appends a second ledger row). Retract/rollback of the ledger insert is also no longer possible: it is already committed when the balance updates fail, so a caller that catches the raised exception and returns an error to the user has persisted an auditable 'transfer happened' record for a transfer it reported as failed. This is a regression introduced by this diff, not pre-existing.

findings.title: Apply balances inside the same transaction as the ledger insert
findings.whyItBreaks: Base committed ledger INSERT + both balance UPDATEs in one db.transaction() (f351d2c app/transfer.py:4-16), so any failure rolled all three back. Head keeps only _record_ledger inside the with-block and moves _apply_balances to line 24, outside it. Two concrete wrong behaviors on live paths: (1) if either UPDATE raises (deadlock, constraint, connection loss, non-existent row on a DB that errors per statement), the ledger row is already committed while balances are unchanged, and the caller sees an exception — so the caller's retry runs _record_ledger a second time and applies the debit a second time, double-debiting the sender against a ledger showing two transfers; (2) the two UPDATEs are now separate autocommit statements, so a failure between line 9-12 (debit) and line 13-16 (credit) permanently deducts cents from from_acct with no compensating credit and no rollback path — money is destroyed and accounts become irreconcilable with ledger. transfer() still returns {"ok": True} with no guarantee that the balances it implies were written atomically.

findings.title: billingDay switched from UTC to local time, shifting billing day buckets
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version keyed the day with getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate; the new line calls getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which resolve against the process's local timezone (TZ env / host localtime). For any deployment not on UTC, every instant within hours of UTC midnight lands in the wrong billing day: new Date('2024-03-01T23:30:00Z') yields '2024-03-02' under TZ=Asia/Singapore but '2024-03-01' under TZ=UTC — so the same event is billed to different days depending on where the process runs, and the function is no longer a pure function of its Date argument. Worse on upgrade: rows/buckets already persisted with the UTC-derived key stop matching the newly computed key around boundaries, so the same activity is either counted twice (new day key created) or missed, and sameBillingDay(a,b) (line 8, derived from this) now splits pairs that were previously the same billing day, changing period grouping. Local time additionally makes the day length 23/25 hours on DST transitions, which is not what a fixed 'billing day' boundary should be. The formatting refactor itself is equivalent (pad() reproduces padStart(2,'0'); the year stays unpadded in both versions), so the timezone swap is the only behavior change and it is unintended in billing code.

findings.title: billingDay now returns host-local day instead of UTC day
findings.whyItBreaks: Base (313eb1c) built the string from getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate; head uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which read the Date in the process's local timezone. For any host whose TZ is not UTC, every instant inside |offset| of UTC midnight is bucketed into the neighbouring day: at TZ=America/New_York, 2024-02-01T01:00:00Z returned '2024-02-01' before and returns '2024-01-31' now (at TZ=Asia/Shanghai, 2024-01-31T23:00:00Z moves from '2024-01-31' to '2024-02-01') — up to ~14 hours of each day re-classified depending on offset. Since billingDay's output is the exported day key used for billing attribution and by sameBillingDay for 'same day' decisions, the same event log produces different day buckets per environment (dev in CET vs prod in UTC), results are no longer reproducible/deterministic, and keys already persisted or reported under UTC cannot be regenerated for those timestamps — a late or replayed event can fall on the other side of the boundary and be charged to the wrong day. At a DST transition the local day is 23 or 25 hours, so the 'billing day' length changes between days on the same data. Nothing in the repo pins process TZ or documents an intentional move to local-time billing.

findings.title: billingDay switched from UTC to host-local time, changing day keys
findings.whyItBreaks: The base body used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate (git show a241ae3:src/billing/day.ts lines 2-4); head uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, so the returned YYYY-MM-DD key now depends on the process TZ (env/deployment host), not on the instant. Substituted: `billingDay(new Date("2024-03-01T23:30:00Z"))` = "2024-03-01" at UTC, but "2024-03-02" on a UTC+9 host; `billingDay(new Date("2024-03-01T01:00:00Z"))` = "2024-02-29" on a UTC-5 host. Two concrete live consequences: (1) `sameBillingDay` (day.ts:7-9, unchanged consumer) now splits the billing day at a moving boundary, so a mixed-TZ fleet or a TZ/deploy-region change assigns the same event to two different billing days — a once-per-billing-day charge is applied twice (or skipped) across the cutover, and previously persisted YYYY-MM-DD keys no longer match the re-derived key for the same record; (2) around DST transitions the local day length is 23h/25h, so a "per billing day" aggregate is over- or under-counted. The only stated intent of the hunk was deduplicating `padStart`; the UTC→local semantic change rides along unannounced on an exported function, and nothing in the repo (no test, no caller, no doc) records local-time billing as the desired contract.

findings.title: Include tenant in profile memo cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: `memo` (src/profile.ts:7) is a module-level singleton shared by every caller, and account names are only unique within a tenant (that is why both `readProfile` and the injected `fetchProfile(tenant, account)` take `tenant`). With `const key = account`, the first call for `('acme','bob')` stores acme's Profile under `"bob"`; a later call for `('globex','bob')` hits `memo.get("bob")` at line 15, returns immediately at line 16, and never calls `fetchProfile('globex','bob')`. The globex caller receives acme's object — wrong `profile.tenant` and wrong `profile.displayName` (cross-tenant identity leakage), and any downstream logic keyed on `profile.tenant` (routing, billing, permission scoping) operates on the wrong tenant. Because there is no eviction/invalidation anywhere in the repo, the poisoned entry persists for the whole process lifetime, so every subsequent request for that account string under any other tenant is served the same wrong profile. The function's own contract — a `tenant` parameter and a `fetchProfile(tenant, account)` callback — promises per-(tenant, account) results; the body no longer computes them.

findings.title: Restore tenant in memo cache key to prevent cross-tenant collisions
findings.whyItBreaks: `memo` is a module-level Map shared by every caller (line 7) and `Profile`/`fetchProfile` both carry `tenant` alongside `account` (lines 2, 12), i.e. an account is only unique within a tenant. Keying by `account` alone makes `readProfile("acme","alice")` and `readProfile("globex","alice")` share one slot: whichever tenant fetches first populates line 18, and every later call for the other tenant short-circuits at lines 15-16 and returns the wrong tenant's Profile object — including its `tenant` and `displayName` — with `fetchProfile` never invoked. The result is order-dependent (setup order decides which tenant wins), leaks tenant A's profile data into tenant B's request path, and any downstream write/routing decision made from `profile.tenant` targets the wrong tenant with no error raised.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenant, causing cross-tenant profile collision
findings.whyItBreaks: `memo` (src/profile.ts:7) is module-global and shared by every caller in the process. Keying it on bare `account` makes the cache identity tenant-independent while the entry it stores is tenant-specific: `Profile` carries `tenant` (line 2) and the fetch is per `(tenant, account)` (lines 12, 17). Substituting the collision: readProfile("acme", "jsmith", f) -> key "jsmith" -> miss -> fetch -> memo.set("jsmith", {tenant:"acme",...}). Then readProfile("globex", "jsmith", f) -> memo.get("jsmith") hits (line 15) -> line 16 returns acme's Profile directly. Two concrete wrong behaviors: (a) the caller receives another tenant's profile data (displayName and all other fields) for an account it never owns in that tenant — cross-tenant data exposure; (b) the returned object's own `tenant` field contradicts the requested tenant, so any downstream tenant-scoped authorization/routing/audit that trusts `profile.tenant` acts on the wrong tenant. The miss path also disappears: fetchProfile is never invoked for the second tenant (line 17 skipped), so per-tenant fetch side effects (logging, quotas, tenant validation inside the fetcher) are silently dropped, and the stale value is pinned for the process lifetime with no way to correct it. Account identifiers are only unique within a tenant here — the signature passes tenant as a separate dimension precisely because they are not globally unique.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: The new try/catch wraps the function's own `throw new Error('missing: ...')` (line 4), so the guard at line 4 is dead code: the error is caught by the same handler that follows it and converted to `return ""` (lines 6-8). Two distinct states collapse into one indistinguishable result: a key that is genuinely absent and a key whose stored value is legitimately the empty string (`store.set('k','')`) both now return `""` — a `Map<string,string>` admits `""` as a valid value, so no caller can recover the difference after the fact. The `string` return type carries no failure channel (no null/undefined/throw), and nothing is logged, so the error is silently lost rather than merely downgraded. The only in-repo consumer, loadAll (src/store.ts:12), previously propagated `missing: <key>` for a bad key and now returns a `string[]` containing `""` entries — a partial/failed read is reported as a fully successful read. Any missing configuration/value is silently read as empty instead of failing loudly, which is exactly the shape that produces bad writes or default-valued reads being persisted as real data downstream. `load` is exported, so this broken contract ships with the module regardless of current callers.

findings.title: Stop swallowing load() errors into an empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: load() is exported and its previous contract was: a missing key throws `missing: <key>`. The added try/catch (lines 2-7) discards that signal and returns "". Because the store type is Map<string, string>, "" is also a valid stored value, so "key absent" and "key present with empty value" now return an identical result — the failure signal is unrecoverable at every call site (no log, no distinct sentinel, no thrown error). Concretely, loadAll() at src/store.ts:12 previously aborted with a `missing: <key>` error and now silently returns an array padded with "" entries for every unfound key, so a caller that persists, renders, or forwards those values writes empty data for what is actually a lookup failure. The catch is also unconditional: any real runtime error from the store argument (e.g. a null/wrong-typed store reaching store.get) is likewise converted into "", hiding bugs behind plausible-looking empty results. This is a public-path error swallow, so the unusable contract itself is the defect even for external callers not present in this repo.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns "" instead of failing
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, a missing key threw Error(`missing: ${key}`) to the caller, which could not be confused with data. The new catch-all (lines 6-8) maps that failure — and any other thrown error, e.g. a TypeError from store.get on a non-Map — to the empty string. "" is a legal value in Map<string,string>, so `load('k', new Map([['k','']]))` and `load('k', new Map())` now return the identical result. The only in-repo consumer, loadAll (src/store.ts:12), therefore stops failing on a missing key and silently returns a [""]-padded array that is byte-for-byte indistinguishable from a store that legitimately holds empty values, so any downstream persistence, reporting, or emptiness check acts on the fallback as if it were real data. Because load is an exported function, the unusable contract (no way to distinguish failure from empty) ships now regardless of current callers.

findings.title: Rename of exported Config.timeoutMs breaks callers and disables the deadline
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported and `timeoutMs` is a required field of it (base src/retry.ts:3,6). Removing it breaks every existing call site written against the base shape at compile time, and for untyped/JSON-derived callers of the head version (the repo has no tsconfig/package.json, so nothing typechecks this) `Date.now() + config.timeout` with a missing `timeout` is NaN, so the guard at src/retry.ts:10 (`Date.now() > deadline`) evaluates `Date.now() > NaN` → false forever: the timeout silently stops being enforced and the loop degrades to a pure maxAttempts retry. The rename also loses the `Ms` unit marker that the base field carried into `Date.now()` arithmetic.

findings.title: retryBackground loops on config.retries; missing/zero value silently calls fn zero times
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground (src/retry.ts:22) is a near-verbatim copy of retry() whose only behavioral difference is the loop bound: config.retries instead of config.maxAttempts (src/retry.ts:9). `retries` was added as a second required field on the shared Config (src/retry.ts:3) that retry() never reads, and maxAttempts is never read by retryBackground(). Any config written in the base shape `{ maxAttempts, timeout }` — or any background task configured with `retries: 0` — reaches `for (let i = 0; i < undefined; i++)`, which is false on the first test, so fn() is never invoked and the function returns normally with no error and no log: the caller's work is silently dropped, indistinguishable from success. Conversely `retries: n` yields n total calls, not 1 attempt + n retries, so the same number means two different things in the two functions and a config authored for one silently changes attempt count for the other. Nothing in the diff adds validation for the field each function does not use.

findings.title: retryBackground loops on config.retries, not config.maxAttempts
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground (src/retry.ts:20-31) is byte-identical to retry (src/retry.ts:7-18) except the loop bound, yet both take the same Config. A caller that configures only the field retry honours (maxAttempts: N, retries: 0) gets `for (i=0; i<config.retries; i++)` at src/retry.ts:22 → zero executions of fn(): the background work is skipped entirely and the function returns void, indistinguishable from success. For any 0 < retries < maxAttempts the same config silently performs fewer attempts on the background path than on the foreground path, with no error and no log. The two fields also carry conflicting conventions (retries = attempts after the first vs maxAttempts = total attempts), so the intended number of executions of the same config object is ambiguous by design.

findings.title: Renaming Config.timeoutMs to timeout silently disables the deadline
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported and `timeoutMs` was its published field name at base (git show 64e1e1a:src/retry.ts:3); the rename at src/retry.ts:4 has no compatibility path. Any caller that still passes `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` (JS entry point, JSON/Env-derived config, `as any`, or a structurally-satisfied object literal spread) now gets config.timeout === undefined, so src/retry.ts:8 computes deadline = Date.now() + undefined = NaN and the guard at src/retry.ts:10 (and :23) can never be true — verified: `Date.now() > Date.now()+undefined` evaluates to false. The timeout therefore stops applying silently rather than failing loudly: fn() is free to block for maxAttempts × its own worst case with the caller's configured timeout ignored. The rename also discards the unit encoding that the old name carried.

findings.title: Exported retryBackground swallows every fn() error with no signal
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground is a new exported (i.e. public) entry point whose entire purpose is to run work nobody is watching. It returns void, `catch { continue; }` at src/retry.ts:27-29 drops every thrown error without logging it, exhausting the loop at src/retry.ts:22 falls out to an implicit `return` with no signal, and the deadline bail-out at src/retry.ts:23 returns as if the work had been done. A caller therefore cannot distinguish "succeeded", "failed all N attempts", or "attempted nothing because the deadline passed" — and on a background path there is no return value, no log line and no thrown error left to surface it, so persistent failures (or the total-skip case above) are silent forever: whatever the background job is meant to trigger (cache refresh, flush, sync, dispatch) is lost while the caller proceeds as if it succeeded.

findings.title: Public Config.timeoutMs rename silently disables the deadline
findings.whyItBreaks: `timeoutMs` is renamed to `timeout` on the exported interface with no compatibility field. Typed callers get a compile break (loud), but any caller that builds the config dynamically (env/JSON/file-loaded object, spread, `as Config`, or plain-JS consumer) still passes `timeoutMs` and no `timeout`. Line 8/21 then computes `Date.now() + undefined` = NaN, and `Date.now() > NaN` is always false, so the guard on line 10/23 never fires: the timeout is silently not enforced at all and the loop runs the full attempt bound. The unit-qualifying name was also dropped (`Ms`), so a caller that keeps passing seconds-as-number into `timeout` gets a deadline hours in the future with no error. Nothing in the repo validates `timeout`, so the failure mode is silent loss of the timeout rather than a rejection.

findings.title: retryBackground treats `retries` as total attempts; 0 never calls fn
findings.whyItBreaks: The loop bound is `i < config.retries`, so `retries` counts total attempts, not re-attempts after the first. A caller who configures `retries: 0` — the standard meaning of "run once, do not retry" — never invokes `fn()` at all: the background work is silently skipped, and because the function returns `void` and swallows errors, the caller gets no signal that nothing ran. A negative or absent `retries` (e.g. from an unset env var coerced by JS callers) behaves the same way. The same shared `Config` also forces every `retry()` caller to supply `retries`, which `retry` (line 9) ignores, so one of the two required attempt fields is always dead — a config value that looks meaningful but is discarded.

findings.title: New public retryBackground discards all failure signals (returns void)
findings.whyItBreaks: `catch { continue; }` (line 27) drops the error object entirely — it is never logged, captured, or rethrown — and the function returns `void` on every exit path: success (line 26), deadline hit (line 23), attempts exhausted (fall out of line 22), and the never-ran case (`retries: 0`). This is a new exported public path, so its contract forces every eventual caller to conflate "background task succeeded" with "it failed N times", "it timed out", and "it was never started". The name `Background` hints at fire-and-forget but nothing documents it, and the call is synchronous, so the caller is right there and could have been given a result; a caller that reports or persists completion after `retryBackground()` returns will report the fallback (success) as real.

findings.title: Handle number in FieldProps.value before using value.length
findings.whyItBreaks: The public prop contract was widened to `string | number` (line 2), which promises the component accepts a numeric value, but the body only implements the string case (line 6). Numbers have no `length` property, so `(42).length` is `undefined` and the rendered input becomes the wrong text `len=undefined` — a silently wrong, unprompted display value, not a failure signal. The base version (`defaultValue={value}`) rendered a numeric value correctly, so this is a regression on the newly permitted input. It is also a compile-level defect: property access on `string | number` raises TS2339 (`Property 'length' does not exist on type 'number'`) under any tsconfig, so the file does not typecheck. `FieldProps` is exported, so the widened signature is the public contract and every existing/potential caller passing a number gets a wrong value rather than an error.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field value before using value.length
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 2 widens the public prop contract to `string | number`, but line 6 (added in the same diff) implements it as `value.length`. For a numeric value, `length` is not a property of `number`, so `(42).length` is `undefined` and line 7 renders `defaultValue="len=undefined"` — every caller that passes a number (which the widened type now explicitly invites) gets a field whose displayed/submitted text is a meaningless literal instead of the value's length. Under TypeScript the same line is a hard error (TS2339: Property 'length' does not exist on type 'string | number'), so the exported component does not compile for any consumer that type-checks the union. The type signature promises numbers are supported; the body computes nothing for them.

findings.title: Field renders "len=N" debug string instead of the value
findings.whyItBreaks: Base behavior was `<input defaultValue={value} />` (git show 9e01d1a:src/components/Field.tsx). Head computes `const label = \`len=${value.length}\`` and passes THAT to `defaultValue`, so for a legitimate string prop (e.g. value="hello") every consumer now renders the literal text `len=5` inside the input instead of `hello`. The component's only job — displaying the passed value — is broken for every existing caller; the edit string the user then submits is the debug artifact. `value` is no longer used for anything but `.length`.

findings.title: Widen to string|number but body still uses value.length
findings.whyItBreaks: The public prop type is widened to `string | number` (line 2), i.e. the contract now promises numeric values are supported, but the body only ever reads `value.length` (line 6). `Number.prototype.length` does not exist, so any caller passing a number gets the string `len=undefined` rendered into the input — a silently wrong result with no thrown error, on top of the regression above. Under any TS compile this is also a hard error (Property 'length' does not exist on type 'number'), so `tsc`/CI on a strict setup fails to build. Callers trusting the declared union get corrupt output rather than a diagnostic.

findings.title: Stop echoing secrets.TOKEN into workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step's only observable effect is `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, which sends the value of `secrets.TOKEN` to the job's stdout and therefore into persisted, publicly-readable workflow logs (this workflow runs on every `push`, and run logs are readable by anyone on public repos / by log-forwarding integrations and artifacts). GitHub's secret masking is a display heuristic, not a storage guarantee: masking is keyed on the exact registered secret value, so an empty/rotated/short token, a step that prints it under `ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG`, or any downstream re-formatting of the value bypasses it, and the raw value is present in the runner's own output stream. The token is never handed to anything that needs it — `make build` on line 13 runs in a separate step and does not inherit the step-scoped `env` from lines 10-11 — so the step leaks a credential while contributing no functionality, i.e. pure supply-chain risk with zero benefit. This is a regression against the base revision, which exposed no secret to the log at all.

findings.title: Remove echo of $TOKEN; it writes a secret into Actions logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step binds `TOKEN: ${{ secrets.TOKEN }}` and then runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, so the credential is emitted to step stdout and stored in the run's downloadable logs (retained per the org/repo log-retention policy, and re-downloadable by anyone with Actions log read access — a far wider audience than `secrets:read`). GitHub's log masking is best-effort, not a safety net: it only redacts exact known secret values and is bypassed when the secret is empty, when a job also has a shorter secret that is a substring, or when the value is truncated/wrapped by the runner, so a bare `echo` of a secret is a real disclosure path, not a cosmetic one. The value is also unused — nothing else in the repo reads `$TOKEN` (`grep -rn TOKEN` hits only this step), and the next step (`make build`) does not receive this env, since step-level `env` applies only to its own step. So the step provides zero functionality and only spreads a credential.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git() spawnSync so large diffs do not fail
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's undocumented-by-this-call maxBuffer defaults to 1 MiB per stream (the deleted 64 MiB value was deliberate). git() is the helper used at line 140 for the full patch (`git diff <mergeBase> <headSha>`) and at line 57 for `diff --name-only`; any PR whose patch exceeds 1 MiB (lockfile/vendored/regenerated files, big refactors) now makes spawnSync kill git with ENOBUFS, leaving res.status = null and res.error set. `res.status !== 0` is true for null, so runGithub throws out of line 140 and every such PR gets "Needlefish: review failed" (line 184-191) with exit code 1 instead of a review — the core path is unusable for large PRs. The diagnosis is also unrecoverable from the check log: the throw at line 39 only prints res.stderr, which is empty in the ENOBUFS case, so the failure text is literally `git diff b44eb97... 21c3b76 failed: ` (res.error, which holds ENOBUFS, is discarded).

findings.title: Bundle.baseSha must be the merge-base used for patch/changedFiles
findings.whyItBreaks: patch (line 140) and changedFiles (line 141) are still computed from `mergeBase = git merge-base baseSha headSha`, but the bundle now reports the raw `baseSha` (PR_BASE_SHA env / `merge-base origin/main HEAD`, line 138). Whenever the base branch has moved since the PR branch was cut — the normal case for `github.event.pull_request.base.sha`-style values — baseSha is not an ancestor of headSha, so the bundle is internally inconsistent: the advertised base describes a different change set than the patch it ships. A consumer (review() and the agent it drives, which is told to verify findings with `git diff <baseSha>..<headSha>` / `git show <baseSha>`) resolving that pair gets main's unrelated commits inverted into the diff (files shown as deleted/reverted that this PR never touched), so findings are anchored to the wrong lines/files and in-scope changes are misclassified; the same holds if baseSha is not present in the checkout. Before this hunk, the normalization at line 139 guaranteed the invariant `patch == diff(bundle.baseSha, bundle.headSha)`.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer in git() so large diffs don't fail the review
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1 MiB; the previous explicit 64 MiB was removed only for git(), while gh()/ghText() keep it. The largest output produced through git() is exactly the review payload: line 140 `patch = git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha], cwd)` (plus line 57's `diff --name-only`). For any PR whose diff exceeds ~1 MiB (lockfiles, generated/vendored code, big refactors) Node kills the child, sets res.error (ENOBUFS / max-buffer exceeded), leaves res.status null and res.stdout truncated/empty. Line 38 then throws `git ... failed: ` with an EMPTY stderr (the real ENOBUFS signal in res.error is never read), runGithub's catch posts a "Needlefish: review failed" failure check with a useless message, and the PR can never be reviewed — a core-path breakage plus a swallowed root cause. gh() retaining its 64 MiB shows the cap was intentional, not incidental.

findings.title: Keep bundle.baseSha equal to mergeBase used for patch/changedFiles
findings.whyItBreaks: The bundle's patch (line 140) and changedFiles (line 141, via changedFileSet) are computed from `mergeBase = git merge-base baseSha headSha`, but the field now carries the raw `baseSha`, which is `process.env.PR_BASE_SHA` when set — i.e. the base-branch tip GitHub recorded, typically strictly AHEAD of the true merge-base once main advances after the PR branches. Line 139 still computes mergeBase, so this is not a dead value: the bundle becomes self-contradictory, advertising a base that is not the base of the presented diff. Every consumer that treats bundle.baseSha as "the revision this patch was taken against" — the same way this reviewer's instructions do, running `git diff base..head` / `git show base:file` to verify hunks — now gets a different change set than the Diff text: main-only commits merged after branching appear as reverse (deleted/reverted) changes attributed to this PR, and files the review quotes pre-change content from the wrong revision, producing findings against code the PR never touched. Before the change all three consumers (patch, changedFiles, baseSha) agreed on mergeBase.

findings.title: Restore 64MB maxBuffer on the git() spawnSync call
findings.whyItBreaks: Dropping maxBuffer reverts spawnSync to Node's built-in default of 1024*1024 bytes (1 MiB). The very next call sites feed large output through this helper: line 140 `git diff mergeBase headSha` returns the full text patch and line 57 `git diff --name-only` the file list. When the diff exceeds 1 MiB (generated/vendored files, lockfiles, large mechanical refactors), Node kills git with ENOBUFS, `res.stdout` is truncated and `res.status` becomes `null`; the guard at line 38 (`res.status !== 0`) then throws `git diff <args> failed: ` with an empty message because `res.error` is never surfaced and stderr is empty for a successful-but-killed diff. The whole review aborts into the catch at line 179: a "Needlefish: review failed" check-run is posted and process.exitCode=1, so the PR can never be reviewed by the tool. The sibling helpers `gh` (line 19) and `ghText` (line 29) still set 64 MiB, so 1 MiB is clearly not intended for the diff-carrying call.

findings.title: Bundle baseSha must be mergeBase, not the raw base ref
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch and the pre-classified file set are computed from `mergeBase` (line 140 `git diff mergeBase headSha`, line 141 `changedFileSet(cwd, mergeBase)`), but the bundle now publishes `baseSha` instead. Line 138/139 exist precisely because these two differ: with `PR_BASE_SHA` set (GitHub's `pull_request.base.sha` is the base-branch tip, not the common ancestor), or when the Actions checkout HEAD is the PR merge ref while `PR_HEAD_SHA` points at the branch head, `baseSha` is not an ancestor of `headSha`. Consumers of Bundle.baseSha (review context, `git show <base>`/`git diff <base>..<head>` verification) then inspect commits that are not part of this PR: base-branch-only changes appear as reverse-direction removals in the "full diff", the reviewer is told a base SHA whose content contradicts the supplied patch, and findings get anchored to files/lines that the diff never touched — while changedFiles and patch still describe mergeBase. Previously the bundle was internally consistent.

findings.title: Restore pinned read-only sandbox on codex exec spawn
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns `codex exec` with `cwd: opts.repoPath` and feeds an attacker-influenced prompt (the diff/context under review) on stdin (src/shared/codex.ts:22-27). Before this change the argv hard-pinned `-s read-only`, so no matter what the child process was tricked into attempting, it could not write. With the flag removed, sandbox mode is no longer set by code and no CodexOptions field replaces it (src/shared/codex.ts:6-9 exposes only repoPath/model/timeoutMs), so the effective permission comes from whatever the machine's codex config/profile declares (`sandbox_mode`, e.g. workspace-write / danger-full-access) or from CLI defaults that can differ by version. That means: (a) the same commit behaves differently on different machines, and any dev/CI box whose config grants write access silently runs the untrusted review prompt with write access to the repo under review and to the user's files — exactly the "reviewed code creates files / escapes the sandbox" failure this harness is designed to prevent; (b) the fix is not compensated anywhere else in the file — there is no `--sandbox`, no approval-policy pin, and no chroot/readonly-mount wrapper. This is a removal of a defense-in-depth security control, not a cosmetic arg reshuffle.

findings.title: Restore read-only sandbox on codex exec args
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns the codex CLI with `input: prompt` (untrusted review payload, i.e. attacker-authored diff/AGENTS-adjacent text) and `cwd: opts.repoPath`, i.e. real user working files. Before this change the argv pinned `-s read-only`, so the model's shell commands could not write anywhere. After the change no `--sandbox`/`-s` argument is passed at all (verified: it is the only sandbox occurrence in the file and no compensating flag, config override, or `-C`/writable-root restriction was added in the diff), so the effective sandbox is delegated entirely to the ambient `~/.codex/config.toml` / CODEX_* environment of whoever runs the review. On any machine whose config sets `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"` or `danger-full-access` (a common configuration for interactive codex use — this is the same binary the user runs interactively, resolved via `process.env.CODEX_BIN ?? "codex"`), a prompt injection in a reviewed diff gains arbitrary file write/execute as the reviewing user, with no approval gate available because `codex exec` is non-interactive. A guard that used to be enforced by code is now enforced only by unversioned host configuration, which is a privilege downgrade, not a refactor.

findings.title: Restore read-only sandbox on the codex exec child process
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns the `codex` agent CLI with `cwd: opts.repoPath` (line 24, the runner's working copy of the repo under review) and feeds attacker-controlled diff text as stdin (line 25). Line 20 previously pinned `-s read-only`, which is the hard boundary that made prompt injection in the reviewed diff non-escalatable: the child could read but not write. After this change no sandbox flag is passed at all, so the effective sandbox is resolved from the ambient `~/.codex/config.toml` / CLI default of whoever runs the agent (commonly `workspace-write` or `danger-full-access` on developer machines and CI runners). Concrete regressions: (1) reviewed, untrusted content can now cause file writes/command execution in the runner repo and any path the process user can reach; (2) the review result is no longer trustworthy, because the child can mutate the very files being reviewed mid-run — including creating gitignored artifacts (`__pycache__`, tmp dirs) that the harness treats as a sandbox violation and aborts on; (3) the security posture silently becomes version/config dependent instead of code-enforced, and unlike the previous behavior, a widened sandbox produces no error (a bad flag would at least trip the `res.status !== 0` throw at lines 40-44), so this fails open rather than failing loudly. Nothing in the repo supplies a compensating default: `git ls-tree -r HEAD --name-only` shows only `src/shared/codex.ts` and `.needlefish/answers.json`, and `rg` for `sandbox|read-only|-s` finds no other enforcement point.

findings.title: Restore merge-base normalization before diffing the PR patch
findings.whyItBreaks: baseSha is `process.env.PR_BASE_SHA || merge-base origin/main HEAD` (line 138). The env value is conventionally `github.event.pull_request.base.sha`, i.e. the base-branch TIP, which is NOT an ancestor of the PR head whenever the branch is behind main. The deleted line `git merge-base baseSha headSha` was exactly the normalization that made both configurations correct; without it, `git diff baseSha HEAD` is (PR changes) minus (everything merged into main since the branch point). Concrete consequences on a normal PR-behind-main run: (a) main's newer work appears in `patch` (line 166) as if the PR reverted it, so the reviewer is fed phantom deletions of code this PR never touched and can return changes_requested -> REQUEST_CHANGES + a `failure` check (lines 178-179, 50-53), blocking a good PR (over-block of the merge gate); (b) those phantom files land in changedFiles/changedPaths (line 141) and pass the inline-comment filter at line 63, so comments are anchored to paths/lines that are not in the PR's real diff -> GitHub rejects the review POST -> the catch at line 96 re-posts a body-only review, silently losing all inline findings; (c) a PR edit that main already contains cancels out of base-tip..HEAD, so real changed lines are invisible to the review while the check is still marked `success`.

findings.title: Diff headSha, not the working-tree HEAD, for the reviewed patch
findings.whyItBreaks: headSha is taken from `process.env.PR_HEAD_SHA` when set (line 137), and the review and check are both keyed to it: `commit_id: headSha` (line 85) and `head_sha: headSha` (line 124). The base revision used `git diff mergeBase headSha` for the patch; now the patch is `git diff baseSha HEAD`, i.e. whatever commit happens to be checked out. When PR_HEAD_SHA and the checked-out HEAD disagree (checkout on the `refs/pull/N/merge` synthetic commit whose tree differs from the real head, or a push landing between checkout and run), Needlefish reads one tree and records an approve/fail verdict, plus every finding's line anchor, against a different commit. GitHub rejects out-of-diff comment anchors, which again routes into the body-only fallback at line 96, so findings are dropped while the check still reports a conclusion for a commit that was never reviewed.

findings.title: Diff/changed-files computed from base tip instead of merge-base
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted line `const mergeBase = git(["merge-base", baseSha, headSha], cwd)` existed precisely because baseSha is NOT guaranteed to be an ancestor of HEAD: when PR_BASE_SHA is supplied by the workflow from the PR base ref (github.event.pull_request.base.sha — the canonical value for that env var, which is the base branch tip, not the branch point) and main has advanced since the PR branch diverged, `git diff baseSha HEAD` no longer equals the PR's patch — it also contains the inverse of every upstream commit merged into main after divergence. Concretely, files this PR never touched appear in `patch` (line 139) and in `changedFiles` (line 140, via `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD` at line 57), so (a) the model is asked to review/revert other people's merged work, and (b) `inlineComments` (line 63) now emits review comments on paths outside the PR diff, which GitHub rejects with 422; the catch at line 96 swallows that error and silently reposts body-only, so all inline comments are lost with no signal. Identical behavior is retained only on the `PR_BASE_SHA`-unset fallback path (line 138 already returns a merge base), i.e. the regression fires exactly in the configured-in-Actions case this adapter exists for.

findings.title: Patch taken from working-tree HEAD while review is bound to PR_HEAD_SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: The old hunk diffed against the resolved `headSha` (line 137, which prefers `process.env.PR_HEAD_SHA`); the new hunk hardcodes the literal `"HEAD"`. Whenever those two differ — the common Actions configuration that checks out `refs/pull/<n>/merge` (or a PR head ref that received a push after checkout) while exporting PR_HEAD_SHA — `patch`, and therefore every `lineStart`/`replacement` line range the model derives, describes the merge commit's tree, while `bundle.headSha` (line 160-ish), the review's `commit_id` (line 84/93) and the check-run `head_sha` (line 120) all describe PR_HEAD_SHA. GitHub anchors RIGHT-side comments on the commit given by `commit_id`, so findings land on shifted lines of a different tree, or are rejected outright — and the rejection is swallowed by the body-only fallback at line 96, so the review looks successful while its inline detail silently disappears. Even in the bundle itself the diff is now self-inconsistent: it claims base..headSha while carrying HEAD's text.

findings.title: Diff PR against merge-base, not against a possibly non-ancestor baseSha
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 138 accepts an arbitrary PR_BASE_SHA (the natural value is the base branch tip, i.e. GitHub's pr.base.sha, which advances independently of the PR head). The deleted line `git merge-base baseSha headSha` normalized it; without it, `git diff baseSha HEAD` (139) and `changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha)` -> `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD` (57) are direct A-vs-B tree comparisons. When baseSha is not an ancestor of HEAD, every commit merged into main after the branch point shows up in the reviewed patch as a REVERSE change: files main added appear deleted, main's edits appear reverted. The model is handed third-party changes as this PR's diff, and line 140 classifies those paths as PR surface, so line 141's changedPaths admits inline comments (filter at line 63) for files/lines that are not in the PR; the primary `POST .../pulls/N/reviews` then fails validation and the catch at line 96 silently downgrades to a body-only review, losing every inline comment while still reporting a verdict. The removed `git merge-base` call was also the only place that errored on unrelated/disjoint histories (it exits non-zero, git() throws at line 39 -> failure check-run + exitCode 1 at 181-190); that fail-loud branch is gone, so a bad base now yields a confidently wrong review instead of an error. When baseSha happens to be an ancestor nothing changes, which is why this slips past a happy-path test.

findings.title: Take the patch from headSha, not HEAD, to match the posted review
findings.whyItBreaks: headSha may be supplied by PR_HEAD_SHA (line 137) and can legitimately differ from the checked-out HEAD (e.g. a workflow that checks out refs/pull/N/merge, so HEAD is a merge commit, while PR_HEAD_SHA is the real head). This change replaced `git diff mergeBase headSha` with `git diff baseSha "HEAD"`, so the reviewed content (patch, 139) and the surface set (140) come from HEAD, while bundle.headSha (165), the review's commit_id (85) and the check-run head_sha (124) point at PR_HEAD_SHA. Result: a pass/fail status and finding line numbers are attached to a commit that was not the tree that was reviewed, so comments anchor to wrong lines (or the review POST is rejected and falls into the silent body-only fallback at line 96). The previous code deliberately used the same SHA the review is posted against.

findings.title: Restore replacer functions in prompt .replace() calls
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace(searchString, replaceValue) interprets $-patterns in replaceValue; the base revision used `() => ...` callbacks precisely to pass the payload through verbatim. This diff replaces all three call sites ({{BUNDLE}} at line 25, {{FINDINGS}} at line 32, {{PATCH}} at line 33) with raw strings, so any $-sequence in the inserted text is expanded against the surrounding prompt: `$&` becomes the literal token `{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`/`{{PATCH}}`, `$$` collapses to `$`, `` $` `` splices in everything before the placeholder, and `$'` splices in everything after it (verified locally). `bundle.patch` is arbitrary contributor-authored diff text and routinely contains such sequences (shell `$'...'` quoting, `$$`, JS/Perl/PHP replacement strings such as `.replace(/x/, "$&")`), and JSON.stringify does not escape `$`. Result: the prompt sent to runCodex is silently mangled — duplicated/remapped instructions and truncated findings — so the model sees a body that no longer matches the review policy, and in the `$'`/`` $` `` cases contributor-controlled text is duplicated across the whole prompt (an injection-amplifying path for a tool whose threat model explicitly treats patch content as untrusted). The failure is silent: nothing errors, the verdict just becomes unreliable (or extractJson/normalizeReview throws on garbled output). The `$$` case is pure data loss and fires even for the benign-looking `$` sequence, e.g. a diff line `PRICE="$$"` is rewritten to `$`.

findings.title: Restore function replacers to prevent $-pattern expansion in prompts
findings.whyItBreaks:
When the second argument of `String.prototype.replace` is a string, ECMAScript expands `$` patterns in it; when it is a function, the return value is inserted verbatim. The `() => ...` arrow form removed in this hunk was not redundant — it is the only thing that made the substitution literal. The substituted values are attacker/contributor-controlled text (`bundle` JSON includes `patch`, `agentsMd`, file contents; line 33 substitutes `bundle.patch` directly), so any `$` sequence in a reviewed diff now rewrites the prompt: `$$` -> `$` (a diff line `pid=$$` is sent as `pid=$`, and `$$`/`$` are common in shell scripts, Makefiles and LaTeX), `$&` -> the literal placeholder, so the model sees an unresolved `{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{PATCH}}` token inside the payload, and `` $` `` / `$'` splice the entire prompt head or tail into the data section (verified: `"HEADER
{{P}}
FOOTER".replace("{{P}}", "a$'+b")` yields `HEADER
a
...FOOTER instructions+b
...FOOTER instructions`). Nothing throws or logs, so `review()` keeps returning a confident verdict computed from a truncated/duplicated prompt — and a reviewed PR can use `$'`/`` $` `` to clone the instruction block, which is a prompt-integrity problem for this tool, not just a formatting nit.

findings.title: Keep fallback review anchored to the reviewed head commit
findings.whyItBreaks: postReview's parameter `headSha: string` (@:79) promises the review is posted against the exact commit the review was computed from; the primary path keeps that promise (`commit_id: headSha` @:89), but after this change the catch-body retry (@:101-112) sends only `event` and `body`. GitHub's POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{n}/reviews treats an omitted `commit_id` as "default: the latest commit in the branch", so the server — not the reviewer — chooses the anchor. Because the review is built from `git diff mergeBase..headSha` (@:143-144) and an LLM review runs for minutes, the PR head can move (or be force-pushed) before the retry fires; the fallback then posts a `COMMENT`/`REQUEST_CHANGES` review attached to a commit nobody reviewed. Concrete effects: a `pass` verdict is displayed/applied as an approval of newly pushed unreviewed code, a `changes_requested` verdict blocks merging on issues the author already fixed, and the auto-dismiss-stale-reviews behaviour no longer matches the review content (previously the review was visibly tied to the reviewed SHA). The check run is still pinned to the reviewed SHA (`head_sha: headSha` @:128), so the check and the review now disagree about which commit was reviewed, and `runGithub` (@:183-184) has no way to detect the mismatch.

findings.title: Keep commit_id in the postReview retry fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: commit_id is optional on POST /pulls/{n}/reviews, so dropping it makes GitHub default to the PR branch's *latest* commit. headSha (src/adapters/github.ts:141-142) is captured once at the start of a multi-minute review and may come from PR_HEAD_SHA, so it can differ from the current branch head (push during review, force-push/rebase that removes the old SHA, merge-commit override). The JSON path at :88-99 still pins commit_id=headSha, so this divergence only materializes on the retry path — i.e. precisely when something is already unusual. Two concrete wrong behaviors: (1) the verdict (pass -> COMMENT, changes_requested -> REQUEST_CHANGES) is submitted against a commit whose diff was never reviewed, so branch protection / the PR UI reflect a review that does not correspond to that head; (2) the failure mode becomes silent — if the old SHA is no longer part of the PR, the previous retry failed loudly, propagated through the catch at :183 into postCheck(..., "failure", "Needlefish: review failed") at :185-192 with process.exitCode = 1; now the retry succeeds, the run reports a normal verdict, and postCheck still pins its check-run to head_sha: headSha (:131), so the review and the check-run for the same run land on different commits. The body text produced by renderMarkdown(result) is base..head specific and is now labeled against a different commit.

findings.title: Malformed findings silently upgraded to synthetic blocking P1s
findings.whyItBreaks: Every `throw new Error("malformed finding: ...")` branch was removed, so a finding that used to be rejected is now fabricate-and-pass: missing/unknown severity ("high", "P4", "", absent) -> severity "P1" (line 98); unknown category -> "bug" (100-102); missing title -> "Untitled finding" (99); missing file -> "" with lineStart/lineEnd 0 (103-105) even though the Finding contract requires a real file+line citation; missing whyItBreaks/suggestedFix -> "" (107-108). Because the default severity is P1 (the blocking band) and confidence defaults to 0, garbage input now produces a confidently-rendered, merge-blocking finding with no anchor, and no caller can distinguish it from a real one. The same lines also delete the previous `strict=false` behavior at normalizeReview (base lines 155-165): invalid findings used to be dropped, now they are emitted, so both prior modes regress; and the exported signature dropped `strict = true`, so any existing `normalizeReview(raw, false)` caller is a TS arity error and, once fixed to one arg, silently flips from drop-bad-findings to keep-everything-as-P1. This is TRIGGER D on an exported path: the error signal is gone, and the fallback value is acted on as real.

findings.title: Removed non-object guard makes null/undefined findings crash
findings.whyItBreaks: The `if (!raw || typeof raw !== "object") throw` guard at base lines 96-98 was deleted, but the body immediately reads `raw.severity` (line 96) and `raw.title`/`raw.category` (99-102). `raw.findings = [null]` or `[undefined]` — a common shape in truncated JSON output — now throws an uncontrolled `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'severity')` out of `raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding)` (line 131). Previously that input produced the intentional `malformed finding: not an object` error (strict) or was dropped entirely (strict=false), so the whole review still completed; now the entire normalizeReview call dies on one bad element with a message that no longer names the input contract.

findings.title: Restore rejection of malformed findings in normalizeFinding
findings.whyItBreaks: Every throw that rejected a bad finding is gone, replaced by defaults, and the only caller (line 131) no longer filters. Substituting real LLM-output shapes: findings:["junk"] or {} → sev=String(undefined??"")="" not in SEVERITIES → severity "P1", category "bug", title "Untitled finding", file "", lineStart/lineEnd 0, whyItBreaks/suggestedFix "" — a fully-formed, evidence-free P1 finding that a severity-based verdict turns into changes_requested (blocks a legitimately clean PR). Conversely severity:"p0 - must fix"/"critical" is not in SEVERITIES and is silently downgraded to the default P1, and a self-labelled "nit"/"P4" is inflated to a blocking P1; in both directions the reported severity no longer reflects the review. lineStart:"abc" or a negative value yields NaN/<=0 where base enforced Number.isFinite && >0, so a finding persists with lineStart NaN, which JSON.stringify writes as null in the stored review artifact (data loss on the anchor). Also, with the `!raw || typeof raw !== "object"` guard deleted, normalizeReview(null) inside findings now throws a bare TypeError instead of "malformed finding: not an object", so the retry/needs_human path can no longer tell the model its output was malformed. The new `Partial<Finding>` parameter type is a carrier that promises a checked shape the body does not check.

findings.title: Re-apply trim normalization to file and category
findings.whyItBreaks: Base normalized these strings before comparing/storing (`String(raw.category ?? "").trim()`, `String(raw.file ?? "").trim()`); the head version does neither, and severity is the only field that still gets `.trim().toUpperCase()`. Consequences on live input: category " security" or "Security " fails `CATEGORIES.includes(raw.category)` and is silently rewritten to "bug", so a security finding is reported under the wrong bucket; file " src/shared/schema.ts " (a very common LLM artifact) is stored untrimmed and no longer string-matches the changedFiles paths, so the finding cannot be anchored to its file. Title is also no longer trimmed while being sliced to 120 chars, so padded titles keep their whitespace. This defect is independent of the validation removal, so it survives even if the author argues leniency is intentional.

findings.title: Do not drop normalizeReview's exported strict parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: `normalizeReview` is exported, and the diff removes its second parameter while simultaneously deleting the lenient branch that parameter selected.
