Existing callers that passed `normalizeReview(raw, true)` or `(raw, false)` now hit a TypeScript arity error ("Expected 1 arguments, but got 2") at the call site, i.e. a build break on upgrade from this shared module; untyped/JS callers compile but silently change behavior: the non-strict mode that previously dropped un-parseable findings now emits them with fabricated P1/"bug"/line-0 values, so the strict-vs-lenient distinction the API promised (and that callers used to trade "fail the review" against "keep the good findings") is unrecoverable.

findings.title: normalizeFinding silently fabricates findings instead of rejecting malformed input
findings.whyItBreaks: Base rejected every malformed finding with a specific Error (base src/shared/schema.ts:96-121: non-object, invalid severity, invalid category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, bad lineStart/lineEnd). Head never throws: a finding with no severity becomes "P1" (line 98), an unrecognized/mis-cased category becomes "bug" (lines 100-102, which also no longer trims/lowercases the input, so a valid category such as " Bug " is now silently remapped), an absent title becomes the literal "Untitled finding" (line 99), and file/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix become "" (lines 103, 107-108). Callers can no longer distinguish "the agent produced a real P1 finding" from "the agent produced nothing recognizable": junk entries are promoted to blocking-severity findings with empty rationale and shipped into the review output. Non-object array elements are worse than before: a null element now throws an unguarded TypeError from line 96's property access instead of the previous explicit "malformed finding: not an object", while a string/number element is silently accepted as an empty object and fabricated. The repo's own sample payload in .needlefish/answers.json is exactly this shape (keys `line`/`severity`, no `category`, no `suggestedFix` on two of three items) — under head all three items become valid-looking P1/P2 findings whose suggestedFix/whyItBreaks are empty strings, which base either rejected or dropped.

findings.title: Restore explicit repo for gh pr view in pre-checkout step
findings.whyItBreaks: `gh` resolves the repository only from -R/--repo, $GH_REPO, or the CWD's git remotes (the shipped step env sets only GH_TOKEN/PR_NUM/EVENT_*, and gh 2.98.0 never reads GITHUB_REPOSITORY — 0 occurrences in the binary). This "Resolve PR refs" step is the job's FIRST step; actions/checkout@v4 runs later (line 42-46), so on any workspace without a leftover .git (fresh/cleaned self-hosted workspace, first dispatch) both calls die with "none of the git remotes configured for this repository point to a known GitHub host". That failure is not surfaced: it sits inside a command substitution used as an argument to `echo`, whose exit status is 0, so Actions' default `bash -e -o pipefail` does not abort. The step succeeds while writing `head=` and `base=` (empty) to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, so checkout receives `ref: ''` and silently falls back to github.ref (the dispatched branch, not the PR head), and the review step gets PR_BASE_SHA=''/PR_HEAD_SHA='' (lines 56-57) — i.e. the review agent proceeds on the wrong/undefined diff instead of failing. Base code (with -R "$REPO") could not fail this way; the empty-string-on-error masking is only reachable because the explicit repo was removed. The pull_request event path is unaffected (EVENT_HEAD is set, so the else branch is skipped) — this hits exactly the documented manual-dispatch path.

findings.title: Restore explicit -R repo for gh pr view (step runs pre-checkout)
findings.whyItBreaks: `gh` resolves the target repository only from --repo/-R, the GH_REPO env var, or a git repo (remote) in the current working directory. This step is the FIRST step of the job (the `Resolve PR refs` block at :26-40 runs before `Checkout PR head` at :42-46), there is no `working-directory`/`defaults` override, and the step env (:28-32) sets only GH_TOKEN/PR_NUM/EVENT_HEAD/EVENT_BASE — no GH_REPO. So on a `workflow_dispatch` run the runner's job workspace contains no git repository and `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` aborts with "could not determine which repository to use"; the manual review entry point (the only path that reaches this branch, since `pull_request` events take the EVENT_HEAD branch at :34) becomes unusable. Worse, on a reused self-hosted runner workspace that still holds a stale `.git`, the call instead resolves to whatever `origin` is left over (possibly a fork or another repo), so PR_NUM is looked up in the wrong repository and the resulting head/base SHAs are wrong — checkout at :45 then reviews arbitrary code. The base version's `-R "$REPO"` (github.repository) was always correct here, including for fork PRs, and also guards against that stale-remote mis-resolution.

findings.title: Restore explicit repo context for gh pr view in Resolve PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: The "Resolve PR refs" step (line 26) runs BEFORE "Checkout PR head" (line 42), so $GITHUB_WORKSPACE is not guaranteed to be a git repo with an `origin` remote. gh resolves a repository only from --repo, then GH_REPO, then the git remotes of the cwd, then the cached `active_repo` config; GITHUB_REPOSITORY is never consulted implicitly, and this step's env (lines 29-32) sets only GH_TOKEN/PR_NUM/EVENT_HEAD/EVENT_BASE after REPO was deleted. On workflow_dispatch (line 24 lets it through; EVENT_HEAD is empty, so the else-branch at 38-39 is the live path), `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` aborts with "could not determine which repository to use", and both `head` and `base` outputs come out empty. Downstream, `ref: ''` at line 45 makes actions/checkout fall back to GITHUB_REF (the dispatched branch, normally main) and PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA at lines 56-57 are empty, so the bot posts a "PR review" computed from the wrong revision. On a self-hosted runner whose workspace happens to still hold a stale clone, it can appear to work by resolving that leftover remote instead of the event's repository - correctness now depends on undeclared runner state, which is exactly why the original code passed -R.

findings.title: Restore malformed-review errors in normalizeReview
findings.whyItBreaks: Base (src/shared/schema.ts:115-131) threw 'malformed review output: ...' for a non-object payload and for missing/non-array summary/findings/checked/residual_risks. Head maps each of those failure modes to an empty value (findings=[], checked=[], residual_risks=[], summary="") and returns normally. Callers can no longer distinguish 'the review agent failed / emitted truncated or off-schema JSON' from 'the agent reviewed the diff and found nothing': any parse failure or omitted key now produces the maximally permissive result — no findings, no blocking residual risks, empty summary — which on a verdict computed from findings/residual_risks yields PASS and lets the PR merge with no review actually performed. A review gate that defaults to pass on error is a silent correctness/security regression, not a robustness improvement: normalizeFinding already coerces individual bad fields, so the array-presence checks were the last real validation of the reviewer contract.

findings.title: Restore malformed-output throws in normalizeReview
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes all five validation throws (base lines 115-129: not-an-object, non-string summary, non-array findings/checked/residual_risks) and replaces them with `Array.isArray(...) ? ... : []` / `String(raw?.summary ?? "")` defaults. normalizeReview is the exported parser for the reviewer model's own output (it returns RawReview, the input to the verdict/gate), so every failure mode now collapses into the same value as a legitimate clean review: `normalizeReview(null)`, `normalizeReview("<unparsed text>")`, `normalizeReview({})` and `normalizeReview({findings: {…}})` all return `{summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}` with no error. A caller that previously caught a thrown 'malformed review output' (retry / needs_human / fail-closed) now receives an empty review with zero findings and zero residual risks — i.e. an auto-PASS. Concretely, if the model emits `residualRisks` (camelCase) or a malformed top-level object, the blocking risk entries (`blocks:true`, which by the review policy are the mechanism that prevents a verdict) are silently dropped to `[]`, and unreviewed code is merged. Failure and 'no findings' are no longer distinguishable at any decision point, and the RawReview/Finding types advertise a validated object the body no longer produces.

findings.title: Restore error propagation in normalizeReview; stop mapping bad output to a clean review
findings.whyItBreaks: Base threw a distinct 'malformed review output' Error for a non-object payload, a missing/non-string summary, or a missing findings/checked/residual_risks array (base lines 115-131). The new body returns a fully-formed RawReview instead: normalizeReview(null), normalizeReview("garbage"), normalizeReview(undefined) and normalizeReview({}) all yield { summary: "", findings: [], checked: [], residual_risks: [] }, and normalizeReview({ summary: "ok", findings: [...] }) with no checked/residual_risks yields the same shape as a genuine review with no residual risks. That empty result is byte-identical to a legitimate 'no findings' review, so a reviewer invocation that returns truncated JSON, a string, or an error payload is indistinguishable from an actual PASS — an unreviewed/failed diff is reported as reviewed and clean, and the loss is unrecoverable downstream because RawReview carries no failure field (schema.ts:68-73) and ReviewResult (75-83) has no error state. It also silently drops a partial review's evidence trail: an agent that omits checked[] loses the proof-of-verification the output contract requires, with no signal that it was missing.

findings.title: Resolve PR head/base SHAs for workflow_dispatch runs
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `Resolve PR refs` step existed precisely because `github.event.pull_request.*` is empty on a manual run: it fell back to `gh pr view <pr_number> --json baseRefOid/headRefOid`. After this change, a workflow_dispatch run (still explicitly enabled by the unchanged job condition at line 24, and the sole purpose of the `pr_number` input at lines 12-14) exports `PR_BASE_SHA=` and `PR_HEAD_SHA=` as empty strings into `tsx src/cli.ts --github --pr N`. The CLI can no longer distinguish "no base/head given" from a real value: it either dies on an unparsable rev, or — the dangerous branch — resolves the diff to an empty/range-less set and posts a review that reports a clean result for a diff it never read. Line 35's hardcoded `BASE_REF: ... || 'main'` compounds this: a dispatched PR whose base is not `main` is fetched against the wrong branch.

findings.title: Restore PR head/base resolution for workflow_dispatch runs
findings.whyItBreaks: github.event.pull_request is absent on workflow_dispatch, so every pull_request context expression below evaluates to the empty string. Line 29 therefore falls through to `github.ref` (the ref the operator dispatched from, normally the default branch) instead of the PR head, so `src/` — which is the tool AND the review input in this self-review job — is the wrong commit; and lines 45-46 pass PR_BASE_SHA="" and PR_HEAD_SHA="" where the base revision (bc76f8d) passed the values resolved by `gh pr view ... headRefOid/baseRefOid`. The dispatch mode is still explicitly enabled (the `if:` on line 24 allows `github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'`), the input is still declared required (lines 10-14), and line 47 still feeds `github.event.inputs.pr_number` to `--pr`, so the job does not fail: it runs the review against non-PR code with a null diff range and publishes the result as a review on the real PR (silent wrong output, plus any PR-head-only code is never actually reviewed).

findings.title: Manual (workflow_dispatch) review loses PR head/base resolution
findings.whyItBreaks: A workflow_dispatch event payload has no github.event.pull_request context, so all three new expressions silently evaluate to empty. Line 29 `github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref` therefore checks out the branch selected in the dispatch UI, not the PR head; since lines 3-5 state the checked-out tree's own src/ IS the tool, `pnpm install` (line 39) and `tsx src/cli.ts` (line 47) then run the wrong code against the wrong tree, while lines 45-46 pass PR_BASE_SHA="" and PR_HEAD_SHA="" where the base version passed real SHAs resolved via `gh pr view` (base file lines 40-41) for exactly this case. The `pr_number` input is still read (line 47) and is documented (lines 12-14) as 'manual trigger; bypasses pull_request webhook', so the intended manual path is now broken and, because the failure is a defaulted empty value rather than an error, it can produce a bogus/empty review instead of failing loudly.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git() spawnSync (1 MiB default kills large diffs)
findings.whyItBreaks: With maxBuffer removed, spawnSync uses Node's default of 1024*1024 bytes for stdout. runLocal calls git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"]) at src/adapters/local.ts:100 to build the full patch that feeds the review bundle; a diff over ~1 MiB (lockfile churn, vendored/generated files, ordinary large PRs) makes Node kill git with error ENOBUFS, leaving res.status === null and res.stderr empty. Line 12 then throws `git <sha> <sha> failed: ` with no cause at all (res.error is never surfaced), so the whole local review hard-fails on exactly the PRs that need review most, and the operator sees a message that hides the real reason. The sibling gh() helper at src/adapters/local.ts:33-37 still passes maxBuffer: 64 MiB, confirming the 64 MiB ceiling on the git path was intentional (it was presumably added for this same reason), so this is an unintended removal, not a deliberate tightening.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git() spawnSync (1 MiB default breaks large diffs)
findings.whyItBreaks: git() at line 11 now runs spawnSync with no maxBuffer, so Node's default (1024*1024 = 1 MiB) applies to its largest consumer: patch = git diff <baseSha> HEAD at line 100 (and name-only at 101 for huge changesets). Any PR diff over 1 MiB — routine for lockfiles, generated code, vendored deps, or long-lived branches — exceeds that limit. On overrun spawnSync kills the child and sets res.error (ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDOUT_MAXBUFFER) with a non-zero/null res.status, so line 12 throws line 13's message built only from res.stderr — which is empty for this failure — so the user gets 'git diff <sha> <sha> failed:' with no cause and the whole review aborts. If instead the output is merely truncated on the running Node version, res.status stays 0, res.stdout is cut mid-hunk, and review() silently receives an incomplete patch: files/hunks past ~1 MiB are never seen, so the verdict can be a false PASS. Both branches are user-facing regressions on the tool's core path. The sibling gh() helper at lines 33-37 still passes maxBuffer: 1024*1024*64, confirming 64 MiB was the intended budget for this exact kind of large output; this change made the two helpers asymmetric.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git spawnSync; 1 MiB default breaks large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: git() is the single capture path for every git call, including the full patch at src/adapters/local.ts:100 (`git diff baseSha HEAD`) and the file list at :101. With the option removed, spawnSync falls back to its default maxBuffer of 1 MiB. As soon as a review target's patch exceeds ~1 MB (routine for vendor/lockfile/generated-code or long-running branches), Node kills the child with ENOBUFS: res.status becomes null (killed, not 0) and res.stderr is empty, so the existing throw at :12-14 emits `git diff <sha> <sha> failed: ` with no reason — the ENOBUFS signal lives only on res.error, which is never read. The core review path is therefore unusable for medium/large diffs, with a message that points the user at git rather than at buffer size. The sibling gh() helper at :33-37 still uses 64 MiB, confirming 1 MiB is not the intended cap for diff-sized output.

findings.title: Publish `failure`, not `neutral`, when the review itself errors
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch block still writes "Needlefish: review failed" / "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR", but the machine-readable conclusion is now `neutral` (line 191). `neutral` is the exact conclusion already used for a successful-but-deferred review (`VERDICT_CONCLUSION.needs_human = "neutral"`, line 53), so any consumer of the Needlefish check run (branch protection required check, merge box, dashboards, triage) can no longer distinguish "review completed and punted to a human" from "review crashed / could not post" — and in the latter case it is a non-red state on the PR head. A PR whose review aborted mid-way (LLM error, `gh api` failure, postReview throw, timeout) therefore loses its blocking signal while the text claims the opposite; the only surviving error channel is stderr/exitCode (lines 195-196), which GitHub does not gate merges on. This is a fail-open change to the review gate.

findings.title: Pass explicit repo to `gh pr diff`; it ignores cwd and $GITHUB_REPOSITORY
findings.whyItBreaks: Every other GitHub call in this adapter is repo-explicit (`gh api repos/${repo}/...` at lines 138, 89, 118) so it works from any directory, and every local-VCS call is cwd-explicit (`git(..., cwd)` at lines 57, 140, 141). `gh pr diff <n>` is a repo-context command: it resolves the repository from the *process* working directory's git remote (or GH_REPO), never from the `cwd`/`repo` values this function is given. If the runner is invoked with a clone path that is not process.cwd() — the case the `cwd` parameter exists for, and the case lines 147-148 assume — the call throws before the try/catch at line 179, so no Needlefish check run is ever created and the PR silently gets no review. Worse, if process.cwd() happens to be a clone of a *different* repository, `gh pr diff N` returns PR N of that other repo and that unrelated patch is fed to `review()` while the verdict is posted to `$GITHUB_REPOSITORY` PR N.

findings.title: Restore failing check conclusion when the review itself errors
findings.whyItBreaks: The only machine-readable merge signal for a crashed review is the `Needlefish` check run. Line 191 downgrades it from `failure` to `neutral`, i.e. an exception is now mapped to a non-failing conclusion, while the summary text on line 193 still promises "did NOT pass". `neutral` is exactly what a *legitimate* `needs_human` verdict already produces (VERDICT_CONCLUSION, line 53), so consumers of the check-run conclusion can no longer distinguish "reviewer crashed / LLM errored / gh API errored" from "review completed, a human must look". GitHub treats a `neutral` completed check run as a non-failing state, so a ruleset/branch-protection gate keyed on this check stops blocking unreviewed PRs — the gate fails open on internal error. `process.exitCode = 1` (line 196) only colours the Actions job's own check, which is a different check name and is commonly `continue-on-error`-ed or absent when the binary is run outside Actions, so it is not a substitute for the conclusion on this check.

findings.title: Derive changedFiles from the same diff basis as the new patch
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 143 switches the patch to GitHub's PR diff (merge-base..head, three-dot semantics), but line 144 still feeds `baseSha` = `pr.base.sha` — the base branch *tip*, not the merge base — into changedFileSet (line 57), which runs a two-dot `git diff --name-only <baseTip> HEAD`. Whenever the PR head is not the merge commit (checkout of `refs/pull/N/head`, or any local run), that list also contains every file changed on the base branch since the PR branched, reported as changes made by this PR. So `bundle.changedFiles` (the reviewer's only structural summary / surface map) contradicts `bundle.patch`, and base-branch-only files get classified with a surface and can be cited as if they were part of the change. The inverse case also silently loses signal: a file present in the PR patch but whose content matches base-tip is absent from `changedPaths`, and `inlineComments()` (line 63) filters it out, dropping the inline comment with no error. Before this PR both values came from the same `git diff baseSha HEAD`, so they were consistent; the partial fix breaks that invariant.

findings.title: Pass explicit repo/cwd to `gh pr diff`
findings.whyItBreaks: `gh pr diff <number>` is the first call in this file that needs ambient repository context: `ghText` (lines 28-34) spawns `gh` without `cwd`, and no `--repo`/`-R` is passed, so the repo is resolved from the *process* working directory's git remote rather than from the `repo` (GITHUB_REPOSITORY, line 133-134) and `cwd` parameters that every other call uses explicitly. Two concrete outcomes: (a) if the process cwd is not a git repo, `gh` errors and the entire review aborts into the catch at line 185 (no findings posted at all); (b) worse and silent — if the process cwd is any other git repo with a gh remote (the tool's own source checkout, another clone), `gh pr diff 42` returns PR #42 *of that other repo*, which is then handed to the model as the patch for the real PR and an APPROVE/REQUEST_CHANGES is posted against the real PR from an unrelated diff. Note also that headSha is read at line 140 and the patch at line 143 from two separate GitHub round-trips, so a force-push between them yields a patch whose lines no longer match `commit_id` (line 85), and the resulting 422 is swallowed by the postReview fallback (lines 96-108) that drops every inline comment without surfacing an error.

findings.title: Restore fail-closed 'failure' conclusion on review-error check run
findings.whyItBreaks: This is the only path that reports "the review never ran" (any throw from review(), gh api, git, or postReview lands here). Changing its conclusion from "failure" to "neutral" downgrades the error signal to a non-blocking one: for GitHub check runs, a completed run with conclusion=neutral is not a failing state for required status checks, so a PR whose review crashed (model/API error, timeout, gh failure) shows the required 'Needlefish' check as satisfied and is mergeable with zero review — the agent now fails open. It also collapses the error path onto the same machine-readable conclusion as a legitimate needs_human verdict (VERDICT_CONCLUSION line 50: needs_human -> neutral), so automation/merge queues reading check-runs cannot distinguish 'human needed' from 'reviewer died'; only prose in `summary` still says it failed, and prose is not a gate. `process.exitCode = 1` (line 196) does not restore this: the workflow job's own check is a separate, differently-named check run from the explicitly created 'Needlefish' one — if the job check were the gate, the explicit conclusion here would be pointless.

findings.title: Keep reviewer independent: run tool from PR base, not PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: Base pinned the tool to a trusted revision (`frankekn/needlefish@main` in `needlefish/`) and only the diff under review came from head; the removed comment states this exists to prevent "a PR from controlling its own review by modifying the tool" (base lines 3-6). Head now installs from the PR checkout (`pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` at line 51, executing PR-declared package lifecycle scripts) and runs the PR's own code as the reviewer (`./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` at line 54) with `GH_TOKEN` scoped `pull-requests: write` / `checks: write` (lines 16-19) on `runs-on: self-hosted` (line 23), i.e. arbitrary PR-controlled execution on long-lived runner infrastructure plus the ability to post a clean/approving review. Concretely: any PR that edits `src/cli.ts` (or package.json postinstall, or the `--github` reporting path) can make the reviewer emit PASS for itself, so a regression or backdoor in the reviewer cannot be caught by the reviewer — the control that protects exactly this file class is gone. Note the `if:` on line 24 only excludes fork PRs; same-repo branch writers are still untrusted relative to `main`, and self-hosted runners typically hold SSH keys / registry tokens beyond this job's declared permissions.

Now a single checkout at line 43-46 puts the PR head at the workspace root, line 51 runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` against that PR's own package.json/lockfile (install lifecycle scripts of PR-chosen dependencies execute on the runner), and line 59 executes `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` — i.e. code imported from the PR diff — with GH_TOKEN (line 56) granted `pull-requests: write` + `checks: write` (lines 16-20) on `runs-on: self-hosted` (line 23). findings.title: Restore case/whitespace-insensitive severity parsing in normalizeFinding
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed line `const sev = String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase();` was the tolerance for the function's actual input: raw JSON emitted by a review model, where "p1", "P1 ", "P0\n" are routine. The new check `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity as Severity)` is exact-match only, so any of those variants now falls through to the else branch and the finding is rewritten to severity "P3". P3 is the non-blocking tier (this module's own contract: only P0-P2 gate changes_requested), so a real P0 data-loss/P1 regression finding is silently demoted and the PR is reported as clean — the opposite of what the base code did (it returned the parsed P0/P1). No error, no log, no flag distinguishes demotion from a genuine P3, so the loss is silent at the aggregate/verdict level.

findings.title: Do not collapse invalid/absent severity into P3 (lowest) default
findings.whyItBreaks: The fallback for a severity that fails validation changed from "P1" to "P3" on an exported function consumed by the review pipeline (src/shared/schema.ts:132 `raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding)` over untrusted model output). A missing severity, a numeric severity (severity: 1), or a novel tier ("P4", "critical") is now indistinguishable from a deliberate P3 — the lowest, explicitly non-blocking tier. The error signal (malformed severity on a finding the reviewer wants merged) is discarded at the public boundary, and every downstream consumer of `Finding.severity` (verdict computation, report ordering, blocking set) is forced to treat a parse failure as 'author judged this harmless'. The previous default was conservative (mid-high, blocking); inverting the default direction means each new malformed-input mode becomes a silent false-PASS rather than a false-BLOCK.

findings.title: Restore severity normalization + fail-safe default in normalizeFinding
findings.whyItBreaks: Two independent safety properties are removed in the same hunk and they compound. (1) The deleted line 96 (`String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()`) was the only tolerance for the input this function exists to sanitize: `normalizeReview` feeds it raw model/CLI-supplied JSON (`raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding)` @src/shared/schema.ts:136), where "p1", " P2 ", "P1\n" or a numeric/absent severity are routine. Those strings now fail the exact-match `SEVERITIES.includes` at line 97. (2) The fallback was changed from "P1" to "P3" at line 99, so every such value — including "p1", which previously normalized to P1 — is silently rewritten to the lowest tier. Because severity is the signal that decides whether a finding blocks a merge (P0/P1/P2 vs P3), a real blocker coming back as "p1" is demoted to a non-blocking note and the PR ships; the same happens for a finding with an omitted/typo'd severity, which used to err on the side of P1. The result is also indistinguishable from an author legitimately emitting "P3": no error, no log, no flag — the failure signal is destroyed at the boundary. Additionally, the exported name `normalizeFinding` still promises normalization while the body only does strict enum matching, so callers have no reason to pre-sanitize.

findings.title: Restore case/whitespace normalization of finding severity
findings.whyItBreaks: raw.findings is unvalidated JSON produced by the model (normalizeReview takes `raw: any` and validates summary/arrays but never severity, so this is the only coercion point). The removed `String(...).trim().toUpperCase()` was doing real runtime work even though `raw.severity` is typed `Severity`: values like "p1", "P0", "p2 \n" were previously normalized into the enum and are now exact-match misses, and every miss is rewritten to "P3" — the least-severe tier. A genuine P0 security finding serialized as "p0" therefore lands in RawReview.findings (src/shared/schema.ts:132) as P3, i.e. the change converts an accepted finding into an ignorable one instead of preserving it, and also drops a previously-matched value that the base version accepted.

findings.title: Do not map unrecognized severity to P3 (fail-open default)
findings.whyItBreaks: The severity field is the review agent's blocking signal (P0..P3 ordering is defined at src/shared/schema.ts:1). An unrecognized/missing severity is an error condition, and the base version defaulted it upward to "P1" so a malformed finding still blocked. The new default is "P3", which is indistinguishable in the persisted ReviewResult from a finding the model actually rated P3 — the failure signal is downgraded to a legitimate value, so a review gate that blocks on P0-P2 passes silently. Combined with the lost normalization in this same hunk, the set of inputs reaching this fail-open default grows from 'garbage strings' to 'any non-exactly-cased value'.

findings.title: Restore GH/GITHUB token stripping before spawning codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Base explicitly built a scrubbed env (`const env = { ...process.env }; delete env.GH_TOKEN; delete env.GITHUB_TOKEN; delete env.GITHUB_API_TOKEN;` @ base src/shared/codex.ts:23-26) and passed it via `env` (@ base:30). Head removes both the scrub and the `env` option, so `spawnSync(bin, args, {...})` (src/shared/codex.ts:23-29) falls back to the default of inheriting the entire `process.env`. The spawned `codex exec` process is an agent whose behavior is driven by the untrusted `prompt`/`input` (src/shared/codex.ts:25) — content from the repo/PR under review. The `-s read-only` sandbox on line 20 only constrains the sandbox's filesystem/network policy; it does not hide inherited environment variables, so any shell/subprocess codex launches can read `$GH_TOKEN`/`$GITHUB_TOKEN` (typically repo-write or higher in CI) and emit or upload it. That turns prompt-injected content into a credential-exfiltration path and silently drops a deliberate defense-in-depth control with no replacement and no change anywhere else in the repo (the diff is 6 pure deletions, patch touches nothing that would move the sanitization elsewhere).

findings.title: Restore env scrub before spawning codex (GitHub tokens leak)
findings.whyItBreaks: Base built `const env = { ...process.env }` and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN, then passed `env` to spawnSync. Head removes both the copy and the `env` option, so spawnSync falls back to its default of inheriting `process.env` verbatim (node:child_process semantics). `runCodex` launches `codex exec` — an agent whose behavior is driven by attacker-influenceable `prompt` content (reviewed diffs/issues) — with `-s read-only` restricting only filesystem writes in `opts.repoPath`, not the environment. Anything the spawned agent executes (e.g. `gh api`, `curl`, a tool call from injected prompt text) can now read `GITHUB_TOKEN`/`GH_TOKEN` from its own environment and use it against GitHub with the CI job's permissions (typically repo contents/pull-request write), which is exactly the escalation the removed lines existed to prevent, and it silently breaks the read-only sandbox's intent. There is no compensating change anywhere in the diff (no network flag, no new proxy/redaction), and this repo is the only consumer, so nothing else re-applies the scrub.

findings.title: Restore stripping of GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN from codex env
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex previously copied process.env and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN before spawnSync. With `env` removed (src/shared/codex.ts:23-29), Node falls back to inheriting the full parent environment, so the spawned `codex exec` child — and every shell command that agent runs under its sandbox — now has the caller's GitHub credentials in its environment. The child's stdin is untrusted text (a diff/repo content fed as `prompt`, src/shared/codex.ts:25), which is the exact prompt-injection surface that sandboxing exists for: `-s read-only` restricts filesystem writes, not reads, so the agent can still read its own environment (e.g. via `env`/`printenv`/`/proc/self/environ`, which a read-only sandbox permits) and place the token in output or use it wherever network egress is allowed. The result is a credential-leak regression on upgrade: any CI/local run where the reviewer process has repo-scope or broader GitHub tokens hands them to model-controlled code. `runCodex` is exported, so every caller inherits this weakened contract, not just one call site.

findings.title: Restore fork guard: self-hosted job now runs untrusted PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: Base line 19 (`if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository`) was the only thing keeping external contributions off this runner. Deleting it means any anonymous fork PR now schedules this job on the maintainer's persistent self-hosted runner (line 18) and executes attacker-controlled input end to end: it checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` (line 23), then `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28) runs lifecycle scripts resolved from the attacker's own package.json/lockfile, then `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34) executes the attacker's source directly. That is arbitrary code execution on a durable, shared host — it can read other repos' checkouts and cached credentials/SSH keys on the runner, and poison node_modules/workdir for subsequent runs (supply-chain persistence, not a one-shot sandbox). It also runs with GH_TOKEN injected (line 33) minted under `pull-requests: write` + `checks: write` on the base repo (lines 11-14), so the untrusted code can post/approve reviews and rewrite check results on real PRs — a permission-boundary bypass. For fork `pull_request` runs GitHub does not expose repository secrets, which is exactly why this guard was the compensating control: GITHUB_TOKEN is exposed and is write-scoped here. The narrowed `permissions:` block does not mitigate code execution on the runner.

findings.title: Restore same-repo guard on self-hosted review job
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted line `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the sole gate preventing `pull_request` events from forks from scheduling this job. The remaining head file has no substitute gate (no `environment:`, no fork check on any step). The job `runs-on: self-hosted` and then, under `shell: zsh -l` (line 27/31 — a login shell that sources the runner's own profile, so any credentials there are in scope): checks out the PR head SHA (lines 20-24), runs `corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` against the attacker's package.json/lockfile (line 29 — arbitrary postinstall code execution), and executes `tsx src/cli.ts` from the attacker's tree (line 35). Any outside contributor's fork PR therefore runs arbitrary code on the self-hosted machine, can read the runner's filesystem and credentials (gh/SSH keys used by this review tool across other repos), and can tamper with the reviewed checkout — a supply-chain compromise path, not a hypothetical. It also makes fork PRs fail noisily rather than skip: on a fork PR `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` is forced read-only, so the `pull-requests: write` / `checks: write` the tool relies on (lines 13-14) cannot post the review, turning every external PR into a red job.

findings.title: Restore fork guard: PR code now runs on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted line `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only guard separating untrusted fork PRs from this job. With it gone, any third-party fork can open a PR and the job (runs-on: self-hosted, line 18) will: (1) check out the attacker's own head SHA explicitly (line 23 `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`), (2) run `corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` against the attacker's package.json/lockfile (line 28), so attacker-chosen packages and their pre/post install scripts execute, and (3) execute `tsx src/cli.ts` — the attacker's own source is the tool in this self-review mode, per the file's own comment at lines 3-5 (line 34) — under a login shell (`zsh -l`, line 32) on long-lived, developer-owned hardware. That is arbitrary code execution on the self-hosted runner plus whatever the runner has cached there (SSH keys, npm/ppn stores and auth tokens, other repos' checkouts, any org secrets exported into the runner env), i.e. runner takeover and supply-chain compromise of every repo the runner serves. The change buys nothing in exchange: for fork PRs the `pull_request` event's GITHUB_TOKEN is downgraded to read-only, so the `pull-requests: write`/`checks: write` at lines 13-14 cannot post the review anyway — the run would execute untrusted code and then fail at the post-review step, giving no review output. Same-repo PRs are unaffected (their head.repo.full_name already equals github.repository), so this line's only effect is enabling the fork path.

findings.title: Stop silently overriding explicit 0 for runner kill durations
findings.whyItBreaks: The only value whose behavior changes is exactly 0 (negatives/NaN already fell back under `>= 0`). 0 is a legitimate, previously honored setting for both env overrides: NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 meant SIGKILL fires on the next tick after SIGTERM, and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 meant stop waiting for `close` immediately (setTimeout(…, 0) at lines 117-124). After this change both strings parse to a finite number that fails `> 0`, so the code returns `fallbackMs` — the timeout kill sequence is silently lengthened from 0+0 ms to the full 5000+2000 ms, i.e. the opposite of what the operator asked for, on every timed-out runner. Because the fallback path is indistinguishable from "unset", nothing is logged or thrown: an existing deployment that pinned immediate hard-kill (CI time-boxing, cleanup of stuck/un-killable runner process trees) keeps running but now blocks ~7 s longer per timeout with no signal that its config was ignored. Negative and garbage inputs still fall back, so no defect is fixed by this edit — only a supported configuration is dropped.

findings.title: Do not discard configured zero in readRunnerDurationMs
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate on line 135 was tightened from `parsed >= 0` to `parsed > 0`, but this is a duration passed straight to setTimeout, where 0 is a legitimate configured value (fire on the next timer tick), not a parse failure. Concretely: NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 (hard SIGKILL immediately at timeout, no SIGTERM grace) now resolves to 5000 @line 3-6 and is consumed @line 124; NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 (stop waiting for child 'close' immediately after SIGKILL) now resolves to 2000 @line 7-10 and is consumed @line 123. So an operator/CI config that asked to shorten the post-timeout wait gets the opposite: up to +5000ms and +2000ms held per timed-out runner, with no way to distinguish 'unset', 'invalid', and 'set to 0'. Because readRunnerDurationMs is exported, this is a public contract change shipped now: every caller (present and future) is forced to conflate a valid configured duration with an error fallback.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so unmapped changed files are reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: Hotspots come from the LLM map pass and are then truncated by `sortByRisk(...).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (line 93), so any changed file the mapper did not assign to a surface, plus every file pushed out by the 6-hotspot cap, now receives no deep pass at all. The removed block explicitly existed so that 'never silently skip a changed file' held, and it computed `covered` from the already-sliced list, so it caught both cases. On head, reviewLarge returns a normal verdict for a PR whose files were never looked at: no findings, no checked entry, no residual risk, so deriveVerdict (line 122) reports PASS on unreviewed diffs — a false-negative merge gate, which is this tool's core purpose.

findings.title: Do not hardcode residual_risks: deep-pass blocks=true gaps are dropped
findings.whyItBreaks: The loop reads only `res.findings` and `res.summary` (lines 103-105) and `candidateMerged.residual_risks` is now the constant `[]` (line 113). Deep-pass residual risks — the review contract's channel for 'I could not verify this sentinel and it feeds validation/persistence/authorization, so I cannot conclude pass' — are unconditionally discarded: the critic receives an empty list inside {{FINDINGS}} (line 116) and therefore cannot carry them into `pruned.residual_risks`, which is the sole input to deriveVerdict (line 122) and to the returned ReviewResult.residualRisks (line 128). Failure ('reviewer hit an unverifiable blocking gap') and success ('reviewer had no gaps') become indistinguishable to every downstream consumer, so the merge gate opens on exactly the diffs a reviewer flagged as un-concludable.

findings.title: Restore per-hotspot fallback: one malformed deep pass aborts entire review
findings.whyItBreaks: extractJson/normalizeReview/runCodex are expected to throw on malformed model output — this file guards that assumption twice elsewhere (lines 56-58, 119-121 'likely malformed output'). With the try/catch removed, a throw from any single hotspot inside the up-to-6-iteration loop propagates out of reviewLarge, so `all` and `checked` built from the already-completed hotspots are discarded and review() rejects: the largest PRs (the only ones taking this path, isLarge at line 30) now produce no review at all from one flaky call, whereas before the failure was recorded as a `[name] DEEP PASS FAILED` checked entry plus a blocks=true residual and the remaining hotspots were still reviewed.

findings.title: Stop discarding deep-pass residual_risks in reviewLarge
findings.whyItBreaks: res.residual_risks from each deep pass is never collected and candidateMerged.residual_risks is hardcoded to [] (line 113), so the gaps sub-reports flagged as blocks:true never reach the critic payload (line 116) and never reach deriveVerdict (line 122). A large-PR review whose hotspot passes said 'cannot conclude pass / file X not deep-reviewed' now ships a ReviewResult with residualRisks: [] and can derive a clean verdict. The verdict/residual-risk surface is the tool's public contract (review() at line 131), so failure is indistinguishable from 'no gaps found' for every caller.

findings.title: Restore per-hotspot try/catch so one bad pass is not fatal
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex/extractJson/normalizeReview on one hotspot can throw (the code base already treats malformed model output as expected — see the throws at lines 57 and 120). With the try/catch deleted, an exception on hotspot k propagates out of reviewLarge and out of review(); every finding already accumulated in `all` from hotspots 1..k-1 is discarded and the user gets a raw stack trace instead of a partial review plus a blocking residual, even though the previous hotspots succeeded.

findings.title: Reinstate the coverage backstop hotspot for unmapped files
findings.whyItBreaks: hotspots is truncated to MAX_HOTSPOTS=6 (line 93) and the deleted 'tail-coverage' block was the only thing guaranteeing that changed files assigned to no selected hotspot still get deep-reviewed. On a 30-file PR where the map pass emits 8 hotspots or mis-assigns a file, those changed files now receive zero review, are absent from `checked`, and produce no residual risk — the exact silent skip the removed comment guarded against, and the review can still be reported as complete.

findings.title: Stop discarding deep-pass residual_risks in reviewLarge
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep pass returns RawReview.residual_risks, but after this change nothing in the file ever reads it (git grep at HEAD shows residual_risks referenced only at lines 66/72/113/122/128, i.e. only the critic's output). candidateMerged is fed to the critic with residual_risks hardcoded to [] (line 113), so a blocking gap discovered by a hotspot reviewer ('this nil sentinel feeds persistence, cannot conclude pass') never reaches the critic and never reaches deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks) at line 122 or the returned residualRisks at line 128. On the large-PR surface — the only surface where sub-reviews can declare partial coverage — the run now reports a clean PASS while the evidence for that PASS was silently thrown away. Base had `residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)` (base:127) and passed `residual_risks: residuals` (base:139).

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop for unmapped changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: hotspots is truncated to MAX_HOTSPOTS=6 (line 93) and no longer compared against bundle.changedFiles (the diff deleted the covered/uncovered/tail-coverage block at base:98-110). Any changed file the map pass omits, mislabels, or drops past the 6-hotspot cut now receives zero deep review, and nothing records it: checked[] gets one line per selected hotspot (line 105) and residual_risks is [] (line 113), so the audit trail claims coverage it did not perform. The deleted comment stated the invariant explicitly ('never silently skip a changed file'). Concretely: a PR with 11 changed files where the mapper assigns 9 to surfaces yields a PASS that never looked at the tail files — the exact case reviewLarge exists for. At minimum a blocks=true residual naming the skipped files is required; the diff removes both the review and the disclosure.

findings.title: Deep-pass throw now loses all completed hotspot findings
findings.whyItBreaks: The per-hotspot try/catch (base:123-132) was removed, so extractJson/normalizeReview/runCodex throwing on any single hotspot rejects reviewLarge. Findings already accumulated in `all` from the previously completed hotspots (up to 5 expensive codex runs) are discarded with the stack, `checked` is discarded too, and the caller of review() gets an opaque parse error instead of a result whose verdict is block with '[name] DEEP PASS FAILED: <msg>' + 'k file(s) not deep-reviewed' recorded. Malformed/one-off LLM JSON is the common failure mode this loop was written to tolerate; large PRs are the most likely to hit it, and there the loss is maximal.

findings.title: Restore or fully remove {{FOCUS}} wiring in reviewLarge
findings.whyItBreaks: Base line 122 performed `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")`, which only exists because prompts/deep.md contains the literal `{{FOCUS}}` token. Deleting that substitution leaves `{{FOCUS}}` unsubstituted in the prompt text sent to `runCodex` for EVERY hotspot on the large-PR path — including the common case where the caller passed no focus at all (the `?? "(none)"` default is gone too), so the model now receives a bare template marker where the reviewer-focus section should be, instead of focus text or "(none)". Nothing in review.ts validates leftover `{{...}}` tokens (reviewLarge only checks `summary`/`checked.length`/hotspot count), so this ships silently. It also removes the last remaining reads of `bundle.focus` and `bundle.deep` (head has 0 occurrences of `bundle.focus`/`bundle.deep`; base had 3), while `reviewSmall` still forwards the whole bundle — including `focus` and `deep` — into review.md at lines 52-55. Result: the same public input changes model behavior on small PRs and has no effect at all on large PRs, which is precisely where a user-supplied focus matters most. The caller still sends these fields (this review's own context bundle carries `"deep": false, "focus": null`), so they are not yet retired from the contract.

findings.title: bundle.focus/bundle.deep become dead config on the large-PR path
findings.whyItBreaks: After this deletion, `bundle.focus` and `bundle.deep` are referenced nowhere in src/core/review.ts (verified: `rg -n 'focus|deep' src/core/review.ts` at HEAD has no `bundle.focus`/`bundle.deep` read), yet reviewSmall still forwards both to the model via `JSON.stringify(bundle)` at src/core/review.ts:54. Result on upgrade: the same public bundle/CLI fields visibly change model behavior for a small PR and are silently discarded for a large PR (no warning, no error, no residual risk recorded) — the map pass also loses the `deep` signal it used to size hotspot selection, so a `--deep` run on a >30k-char patch is indistinguishable from a shallow one. Silently ignoring an accepted public flag is the defect, independent of any future caller.

findings.title: Honor or reject bundle.focus/deep on the large-PR path
findings.whyItBreaks: `focus` and `deep` are still Bundle inputs (the same fields the caller populates — the bundle shape carries `focus`/`deep`), but reviewLarge now consumes neither: mapBundle (lines 83-89) drops them so the map/blast-radius pass can no longer weigh the requested focus when picking hotspots, and the `{{FOCUS}}` substitution at old line 122 is gone, so `--focus` has zero effect on a large PR while reviewSmall (line 52-55, serializes the *whole* bundle into review.md) still applies it. The failure is silent: no error, no warning, the review returns as if the focus had been considered. Worse, prompts/deep.md is not touched by this diff, so the `{{FOCUS}}` placeholder it was written to fill is still in the template and is now sent to the model verbatim as an unsubstituted token.

findings.title: formatDuration can render "Xm 60s" — seconds carry into minutes was lost
findings.whyItBreaks: minutes is floored from raw ms (line 90) while seconds is rounded from the remainder (line 91), so the two are computed on different bases. Whenever ms % 60000 >= 59500, Math.round((ms%60000)/1000) yields 60 and the function returns a non-canonical duration: ms=119500 (1m 59.5s) -> `"1m 60s"`, ms=179600 -> `"2m 60s"`, ms=59500 -> `"60s"`. The base implementation rounded total seconds first (Math.round(ms/1000) then floor/60), so the carry was always correct and produced `"2m 0s"` / `"1m 0s"`. Both call sites emit this string verbatim into the rendered review report (per-call stats at line 75, `total ...` at line 80), so roughly 500ms of every 60s of measured duration (~0.8% of renders, per stat entry plus the total) prints an impossible time. A consumer or human reading `1m 60s` cannot tell it from a formatting/parsing fault in the report.

findings.title: formatDuration can emit 60 seconds instead of carrying into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: minutes is floored from raw ms while seconds is rounded from the remainder, so the two are computed on different bases. For ms % 60000 >= 5000 (i.e. remainder in [59.5s, 60s)) Math.round yields 60: ms=59_900 -> '60s' (base: '1m 0s'), ms=119_900 -> '1m 60s', ms=4_199_500 -> '69m 60s'. Those strings reach the rendered review body at render.ts:75 and render.ts:80 ('total 1m 60s'), so every PR comment whose call/total duration lands in that ~1s-per-minute window shows an impossible duration, and the sequence is non-monotonic ('1m 59s' -> '1m 60s' -> '2m 0s'). The base version rounded totalSeconds once and then split with floor/%, which carried the rounded-up second into the minutes field; that carry is what this rewrite dropped.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes in formatDuration
findings.whyItBreaks: seconds is computed independently of minutes, so any duration whose (ms % 60000) is >= 59500 renders a 60 in the seconds slot. Substituting real values: ms=119500 -> minutes=floor(119500/60000)=1, seconds=Math.round(59500/1000)=Math.round(59.5)=60 -> "1m 60s" (base code: totalSeconds=round(119.5)=120 -> "2m 0s"); ms=59600 -> minutes=0, seconds=60 -> "60s" (base: "1m 0s"). The same applies at every minute boundary (e.g. 179500 -> "2m 60s", 1199500 -> "19m 60s"). Both call sites, src/shared/render.ts:75 (per-call duration) and src/shared/render.ts:80 (total duration), print this string directly into the review report, so a malformed/non-normalized duration can be published in the PR comment whenever a model call or total run lands just under a minute boundary — a common shape for long-running or timeout-adjacent calls. The base implementation rounded the total first precisely to avoid this; the new form is strictly worse and fixes nothing.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0 and empty strings despite positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The only changed line flips `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, but the exported symbol name `parsePositiveInteger` and the surviving error message `"${label} requires a positive integer"` (line 33) are unchanged, so the public contract still promises a value >= 1. The body now returns 0 for `"0"` and, because `Number("")`/`Number("   ")` are 0, also returns 0 for an empty or whitespace-only env var / CLI argument that used to fail validation. Every consumer of this shared helper (e.g. RunnerOptions.timeoutMs, RunStat.attempts-shaped retry/limit values, which are exactly the integers this validator exists to gate) relies on the returned value being >= 1; a caller can no longer distinguish "the user supplied a missing/zero value" from a legitimate one and will proceed with 0 timeouts / 0 attempts / 0-size loops instead of surfacing the error. The binding for `<= 0` existed only to reject this class of value, so the change silently discards that validation while keeping the promise text. This is a defect in the exported contract itself, independent of whether any consumer is present in this snapshot.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger accepts 0 and empty strings, breaking its positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` makes the guard a non-negative check while the exported symbol name (L30) and the thrown message (L33, "requires a positive integer") still promise positivity, so the contract is now false for every caller: `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` returns 0 instead of throwing. It is worse than just allowing zero, because `Number("")` and `Number("  \n")` are exactly 0 and `Number.isInteger(0)` is true, so an unset/empty env var or blank flag value now parses successfully as 0 instead of erroring. Downstream, any caller feeding this into RunStat.attempts (L17) or RunnerOptions.timeoutMs (L8) receives a legitimate-looking 0 — zero attempts / zero-timeout — and cannot distinguish "operator left it blank" from "operator chose 0", so the misconfiguration is silently persisted into run accounting instead of failing at parse time. There are no other files in this repo (src/shared/runner.ts is the only source file), so the helper exists purely as an exported API for external callers, which is where the broken promise lands.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0/blank input despite positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing the bound from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` makes the exported helper return 0 for input "0", and — because the guard sits on `Number(value)` — also for "" and " " (`Number("") === 0`, `Number.isInteger(0) === true`). Previously those inputs threw. The function name and the error message at line 33 (`${label} requires a positive integer`) still promise a strictly positive result, so every caller of this public API receives a value the contract declares impossible: it cannot distinguish "unset / blank flag" from an explicit 0, and any downstream loop/retry/timeout that consumes the result (e.g. `RunnerOptions.timeoutMs`, `RunStat.attempts` in this same module, which a `parsePositiveInteger(...)` call feeds) silently gets 0 — zero attempts, or a zero-ms timeout — instead of the error the message text still claims will be raised.
